tagline: A beam of fast electrons passes through a specimen thin enough to be transparent to them, giving sub-nanometre detail of cells, organelles and macromolecules.
principle: Electrons accelerated through a potential V have a de Broglie wavelength of a few picometres (2.5 pm at 200 kV, 1.97 pm at 300 kV), roughly five orders of magnitude shorter than visible light. Diffraction is therefore not what limits resolution; the limits are the aberrations of magnetic lenses, specimen preparation and radiation damage.

Magnetic lenses are always convex (positive spherical aberration, Cs, typically 1-3 mm for an uncorrected objective), so they are used at very small apertures, around 10 mrad. Scherzer showed that the best uncorrected point resolution is about 0.66 Cs^(1/4) λ^(3/4), which is 0.2-0.3 nm for a modern instrument. Hexapole aberration correctors (Haider and Rose, 1998) cancel Cs and push materials TEM below 0.1 nm.

Contrast in biological TEM comes from two mechanisms. Amplitude (scattering) contrast arises when heavy-metal stains such as osmium, uranium and lead scatter electrons to high angles where they are removed by the objective aperture, so stained membranes look dark. Phase contrast arises because the specimen shifts the phase of the electron wave; it is converted into intensity by deliberately defocusing the lens, which is described by the contrast transfer function (CTF). Unstained or frozen samples rely almost entirely on phase contrast.

Scanning TEM (STEM) focuses the beam into a sub-nanometre probe and rasters it. An annular dark-field detector collecting electrons scattered to high angles (HAADF) gives intensity roughly proportional to Z^1.7, so heavy atoms and stains stand out with directly interpretable contrast. STEM also enables spatially resolved spectroscopy: energy-dispersive X-ray analysis (EDX) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) map elements such as phosphorus, iron or calcium.

Because electrons interact strongly with matter, specimens must be thin: about 50-100 nm for plastic sections at 80-120 kV, with an inelastic mean free path in ice of roughly 300-400 nm at 300 kV. Thick specimens give multiple and inelastic scattering, which blurs the image through chromatic aberration (an energy filter removes inelastically scattered electrons).
light_path: Electron source: a thermionic tungsten or LaB6 filament, or a field emission gun (FEG) with higher brightness and coherence, emits electrons under ultra-high vacuum.
Acceleration: the electrons are accelerated through 80-300 kV in the gun and accelerator stack.
Condenser lenses and condenser aperture set the illuminated area, convergence and dose rate on the specimen (parallel illumination for TEM, a focused probe for STEM).
Specimen: a thin section or particle layer on a 3 mm copper or gold grid, held in a goniometer stage that can tilt.
Objective lens and objective aperture: form the first magnified image and back focal plane diffraction pattern; the aperture removes widely scattered electrons and generates amplitude contrast.
Optional energy filter removes inelastically scattered electrons (zero-loss imaging) or selects a loss window (EELS, elemental mapping).
Intermediate and projector lenses magnify the image (or the diffraction pattern) onto the detector.
Detector: a phosphor screen, a scintillator-coupled CCD/CMOS, or a direct electron detector that counts individual electrons; in STEM, annular detectors record scattered electrons pixel by pixel.

resolution.xy: ~0.1-0.3 nm instrumental; ~1-2 nm in practice for stained plastic sections
resolution.z: projection through the full section thickness (50-100 nm); 3D needs tomography or serial sections
resolution.why: Lens aberrations (Cs, Cc), specimen thickness, stain granularity (~1-2 nm) and radiation damage limit biological resolution, not the electron wavelength.

equations.name: Relativistic electron wavelength
equations.formula: λ = h / √(2 m₀ e V (1 + e V / (2 m₀ c²)))
equations.meaning: De Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through V volts; the relativistic term matters above ~50 kV. λ ≈ 3.70 pm at 100 kV, 2.51 pm at 200 kV, 1.97 pm at 300 kV.

equations.name: Scherzer point resolution
equations.meaning: Best interpretable resolution of an uncorrected phase-contrast TEM at Scherzer defocus Δf ≈ −1.2 √(Cs λ).

equations.name: Phase contrast transfer function
equations.formula: CTF(k) = −sin(π λ Δf k² − (π/2) Cs λ³ k⁴)
equations.meaning: How strongly each spatial frequency k is transferred into image contrast at defocus Δf; it oscillates in sign, so some frequencies are inverted and some lost at the zeros.

equations.name: Chromatic defocus spread
equations.meaning: Energy spread ΔE of the beam (or energy lost in the specimen) produces a spread of focus that damps high-resolution information; Cc is the chromatic aberration coefficient.

equations.name: HAADF-STEM contrast
equations.meaning: High-angle scattering approaches Rutherford behaviour, so dark-field STEM intensity rises steeply with atomic number.

key_numbers.value: 50-90 nm (silver-grey to pale gold interference colour)

key_numbers.label: Column vacuum
key_numbers.value: ~10⁻⁵ Pa near specimen, ~10⁻⁸ Pa at a FEG

strengths: Highest routine resolution of any imaging method for cellular ultrastructure (membranes, vesicles, cytoskeleton, synapses).
Heavy-metal staining gives unambiguous membrane contrast; the 'reference' view of the cell.
Immunogold labelling gives molecular identity at ~10-20 nm precision.
STEM-EDX/EELS adds elemental mapping; electron tomography adds 3D.
limitations: Samples must be thin, in vacuum and (unless frozen) chemically fixed, dehydrated and stained: no live imaging.
Sees only a tiny volume: a 70 nm section of one cell is a small, possibly unrepresentative sample.
Contrast reports stain distribution, not native density; fixation and dehydration can extract lipids and distort membranes.
Expensive instruments and slow, skilled sample preparation.
best_for: Ultrastructure of organelles, synapses, cilia, cell junctions and pathogens.
Confirming morphology suggested by light microscopy (e.g. mitochondrial cristae, autophagosomes).
Negative-stain screening of purified proteins and virus particles before cryo-EM.
Immunogold localisation and elemental mapping (STEM-EDX).
sample_prep: Classic route: aldehyde fixation (glutaraldehyde, often with paraformaldehyde), osmium tetroxide post-fixation, en bloc uranyl acetate, graded ethanol or acetone dehydration, epoxy resin embedding (Epon, Spurr), ultramicrotomy to 50-90 nm with a diamond knife, collection on copper grids, then uranyl acetate and lead citrate counterstaining. Better preservation: high-pressure freezing followed by freeze substitution, which immobilises the cell in milliseconds. Negative stain for particles: adsorb protein on glow-discharged carbon film and embed in 1-2% uranyl acetate or formate. Immunogold: mild fixation, Lowicryl or LR White resin or Tokuyasu cryosections, antibodies with 5-15 nm colloidal gold.
tips: Glow-discharge carbon-coated grids immediately before use so that sections or particles spread evenly.
Judge section thickness by interference colour during cutting; grey-silver (~60-70 nm) is a good compromise between contrast and resolution.
Lead citrate precipitates with CO₂; stain in a CO₂-free chamber with NaOH pellets and rinse with boiled water.
Pre-irradiate (beam-stabilise) plastic sections at low magnification before recording to avoid drift and shrinkage during acquisition.
Use a small objective aperture for contrast at low magnification and a larger one for high resolution; check eucentric height before tilting.
Record a calibration grating (e.g. cross-grating replica) to verify pixel size at each magnification you publish.
pitfalls: Fixation artefacts: shrunken or swollen organelles, extracted cytoplasm and wavy membranes from slow aldehyde fixation or osmotic mismatch; compare with high-pressure frozen material.
Stain precipitates: electron-dense dots of lead carbonate or uranyl phosphate crystals that can be mistaken for gold particles or granules.
Knife chatter and compression: periodic thickness bands and sections compressed along the cutting direction by 10-30%.
Beam damage: holes, bubbling or mass loss in resin and unfixed areas under high dose.
Selective sampling: a few striking images from one section are not quantification; use stereology and systematic random sampling.

quiz.q: Why can't a TEM with a 2 pm wavelength resolve 2 pm details?
quiz.a: Magnetic lenses have large spherical and chromatic aberrations that cannot be cancelled with simple round lenses, so apertures must be tiny (~10 mrad) and the Scherzer resolution ends up ~0.2 nm. In biology, stain grain, specimen thickness, beam damage and preparation artefacts further limit useful resolution to ~1-2 nm.

quiz.q: What is the difference between amplitude and phase contrast in TEM?
quiz.a: Amplitude contrast comes from electrons scattered by heavy-metal stain being removed by the objective aperture, so stained regions appear dark. Phase contrast comes from interference between scattered and unscattered waves, made visible by defocus and described by the CTF; it dominates for unstained, thin or frozen specimens.

quiz.q: When would you choose STEM over conventional TEM?
quiz.a: For thick sections (STEM tolerates chromatic blur better), for directly interpretable Z-contrast with HAADF, and for elemental mapping by EDX or EELS. Conventional TEM is faster for routine imaging of thin sections.

quiz.q: How would you avoid fixation artefacts in an ultrastructural study?
quiz.a: Use high-pressure freezing and freeze substitution rather than chemical fixation where possible, keep osmolarity matched, fix quickly and include controls; report sampling and quantify with stereology rather than selected images.

tagline: A focused electron probe is scanned over a surface and the secondary or backscattered electrons it releases build up an image with nanometre resolution and great depth of field.
principle: The SEM forms a small electron probe (about 1-5 nm with a field emission gun) and rasters it across the specimen. It is not an imaging microscope in the optical sense: each pixel is the signal measured while the beam sits on one spot, so resolution is set by probe size and by the volume from which the signal escapes.

Primary electrons, typically at 1-30 kV, penetrate and scatter inside the specimen in a pear-shaped interaction volume whose depth ranges from tens of nanometres at 1 kV to several micrometres at 20 kV in biological material (Kanaya-Okayama range). Lower voltage gives smaller interaction volume, more surface detail and less charging.

Secondary electrons (SE, below 50 eV) escape only from the top few nanometres, so they report topography; edges and tilted surfaces look bright because more of the interaction volume lies near the surface (edge effect). They are collected by the Everhart-Thornley detector or by in-lens detectors.

Backscattered electrons (BSE) are primary electrons scattered back out with high energy; their yield rises with atomic number, giving compositional contrast. This is the signal used to image heavy-metal-stained resin blocks in volume EM, and to see immunogold on a surface.

Insulating samples accumulate charge that deflects the beam and distorts the image. Solutions are conductive coating (2-10 nm of gold-palladium, platinum or carbon), low accelerating voltage near the charge-balance point, or variable-pressure/environmental modes where gas ions neutralise charge. The small convergence angle gives a depth of field hundreds of times that of a light microscope at equal magnification.
light_path: Electron gun (tungsten, LaB6, or cold or Schottky field emission) produces the beam.
Acceleration to 0.5-30 kV; beam deceleration modes can lower the landing energy further.
Condenser lenses demagnify the source; the aperture sets probe current and convergence angle.
Scan coils deflect the beam in a raster across the sample.
Objective (final) lens focuses the probe to a few nanometres on the specimen surface at a chosen working distance.
Specimen interaction produces secondary electrons, backscattered electrons, X-rays and cathodoluminescence.
Detectors (Everhart-Thornley, in-lens SE, annular BSE, EDX) collect the signal, which is mapped to pixel brightness synchronised with the scan.

resolution.xy: ~1-3 nm for a field-emission SEM (SE); ~3-10 nm practical on coated biological samples
resolution.z: surface technique; information depth from ~1-10 nm (SE) to hundreds of nm (BSE at high kV)
resolution.why: Probe diameter (lens aberrations and source brightness), interaction volume and signal escape depth, coating grain and charging.

equations.name: Kanaya-Okayama electron range
equations.meaning: Approximate depth of the interaction volume, with E in keV, A atomic weight (g/mol), Z atomic number and ρ density (g/cm³). Range grows steeply with voltage and falls in dense, heavy material.

equations.name: Depth of field
equations.meaning: d is the acceptable blur (pixel size) and α the probe convergence semi-angle (~1-10 mrad), so D is micrometres to millimetres, far above light microscopy.

equations.name: Signal yield balance
equations.formula: η + δ = 1 at the charge-balance energy E₂
equations.meaning: When backscatter (η) and secondary (δ) yields together equal the incoming current, an insulator does not charge; for many biological materials E₂ is ~1-2 kV.

equations.name: Electron wavelength
equations.meaning: At 1 kV λ ≈ 39 pm; diffraction is not limiting, but low voltage enlarges the probe through chromatic aberration.

Sputter coat

key_numbers.label: FEG-SEM resolution
key_numbers.value: ~1 nm at 15 kV, ~1.5-2 nm at 1 kV

strengths: Striking three-dimensional-looking images of surfaces, cells, tissues and whole organisms.
Huge range of magnification (10× to >500,000×) and large depth of field.
Large specimens (centimetres) can be imaged; little thin-sectioning required.
BSE and EDX add compositional and elemental information; the basis for array tomography and block-face volume EM.
limitations: Surface only (SE); internal structure needs fracturing, sectioning or milling.
Conventional SEM requires dry, fixed, conductive samples in vacuum.
Charging, beam damage and coating artefacts can obscure fine detail.
Resolution generally poorer than TEM for biological macromolecules.
best_for: Cell surface morphology: microvilli, cilia, filopodia, extracellular matrix, biofilms.
Tissue topography and organ surfaces, insects, plants and biomaterials.
Imaging heavy-metal-stained sections or block faces with BSE (array tomography, SBF-SEM).
Elemental mapping of particles, minerals and implants with EDX.
sample_prep: Fix in glutaraldehyde, post-fix in osmium (optionally with OTO, osmium-thiocarbohydrazide-osmium, to increase conductivity), dehydrate through graded ethanol, dry by critical point drying with CO₂ (or hexamethyldisilazane for small samples) to avoid surface tension collapse, mount on stubs with carbon tape or silver paint, and sputter coat 2-10 nm metal. Cryo-SEM plunges or high-pressure freezes the sample, fractures and optionally sublimes ice before imaging cold. Variable-pressure or environmental SEM can image hydrated, uncoated material at reduced resolution.
tips: Start at low kV (1-3 kV) for uncoated or lightly coated biology to reduce charging and maximise surface detail.
Ground the specimen well: carbon tape, silver paint bridges from sample edge to stub.
Use the in-lens SE detector at short working distance for highest resolution; use the Everhart-Thornley detector for shadowed topography.
Reduce scan dwell and use frame or line integration to beat charging; slow scans give more signal but more charging and drift.
Correct astigmatism at higher magnification than you will record, and focus on a feature at the same height.
Keep critical point dryer CO₂ exchanges complete; residual ethanol causes cracking and collapse.
pitfalls: Charging: bright streaks, image shifting, banding and black-white 'flares' along scan lines; reduce kV, coat, or use charge compensation.
Drying artefacts: collapsed or cracked cells and shrunken tissue from air drying or incomplete critical point drying.
Coating artefacts: grainy decoration or filled fine features when the coat is too thick.
Contamination: dark rectangles from hydrocarbon deposition where the beam dwelt; plasma-clean samples and holders.
Edge effect and shadowing can be misread as true brightness or composition differences.

quiz.q: Why do secondary electrons give topographic contrast?
quiz.a: SEs have energies below 50 eV and escape only from the top few nanometres. At edges and tilted facets more of the interaction volume lies within that escape depth, so more SEs leave and the region looks bright; the detector position adds a shadowing effect.

quiz.q: Your uncoated cell sample is charging. What do you do?
quiz.a: Lower kV towards the charge-balance energy (~1-2 kV), reduce probe current, use faster scans with integration, improve grounding, use variable-pressure or charge compensation, or coat with a few nanometres of metal or carbon. For volume EM, increase conductivity with OTO staining or use focal charge compensation.

quiz.q: SE versus BSE imaging: when do you use each?
quiz.a: SE for surface topography at high resolution. BSE for compositional (Z) contrast: heavy-metal-stained sections, block faces, immunogold labels and mineral phases. BSE comes from deeper, so it has lower surface resolution at high kV.

quiz.q: Why critical point drying?
quiz.a: Air drying passes through a liquid-gas interface whose surface tension collapses delicate structures. Replacing water with ethanol, then liquid CO₂, and taking CO₂ above its critical point (31 °C, 7.4 MPa) removes the liquid without an interface.

tagline: Purified macromolecules are frozen in thin vitreous ice, imaged at low dose, and tens of thousands to millions of noisy particle images are aligned and averaged into a 3D map, often at near-atomic resolution.
principle: Single-particle cryo-EM images many copies of the same complex trapped in random orientations in a ~20-60 nm film of vitreous (non-crystalline) ice. Rapid plunging into liquid ethane cools water faster than ~10⁵ K/s, so it solidifies as a glass without ice crystals and the protein stays hydrated and in near-native conformations.

Biological matter is made of light atoms and is destroyed by electrons, so images are recorded with a total dose of only ~40-60 e⁻/Å². Each particle image therefore has a very low signal-to-noise ratio and contrast comes almost entirely from weak phase contrast, made visible by imaging 0.5-2.5 µm under focus. The contrast transfer function (CTF) multiplies the image Fourier transform by an oscillating function whose zeros depend on defocus; it is estimated per micrograph (CTFFIND, Gctf) and corrected during reconstruction.

Direct electron detectors (from ~2012) count individual electrons at high frame rates, so each exposure is a movie of 40-60 frames. Beam-induced motion and stage drift are corrected by aligning frames (motion correction), and frames can be weighted by dose so that high-resolution information from early, less damaged frames counts more.

Particles are picked, sorted by 2D classification, and assigned orientations and positions by projection matching or maximum-likelihood/Bayesian methods (RELION, cryoSPARC). By the projection-slice theorem each 2D projection is a central slice of the 3D Fourier transform, so many orientations fill Fourier space and the 3D map is reconstructed. 3D classification separates conformational and compositional states, which is a key advantage over crystallography.

Resolution is reported from the Fourier shell correlation (FSC) between two independently refined half-maps, conventionally at FSC = 0.143. The B-factor describes how fast signal falls with resolution due to motion, damage, alignment errors and heterogeneity; the number of particles needed grows exponentially with 1/d², which is why better ice, detectors and alignment mattered so much for the 2013-2014 resolution revolution.
light_path: Field emission gun (often cold FEG) produces a coherent beam at 200-300 kV.
Condenser system sets parallel illumination and a low dose rate (~1-15 e⁻/pixel/s on a counting camera).
Low-dose mode: search at low magnification, focus on an adjacent area, then expose only the target hole.
Specimen: holey carbon or gold grid with vitreous ice across the holes, held at liquid-nitrogen temperature in an autoloader.
Objective lens images the ice layer at a set under-focus; a phase plate is optional.
Energy filter (typically 10-20 eV slit) removes inelastically scattered electrons to improve contrast.
Direct electron detector records a dose-fractionated movie in counting or super-resolution mode.
Automated software (EPU, SerialEM) collects thousands of movies per day across many holes and grid squares.

resolution.xy: ~1.2-4 Å for well-behaved complexes; record ~1.2 Å (apoferritin)
resolution.z: isotropic 3D map if orientations are well distributed
resolution.why: Radiation damage and low SNR, particle number and B-factor, conformational heterogeneity, preferred orientation, beam-induced motion and ice quality; particles below ~50 kDa are hard to align.

equations.name: Relativistic electron wavelength
equations.formula: λ = h / √(2 m₀ e V (1 + e V / (2 m₀ c²)))
equations.meaning: 1.97 pm at 300 kV; wavelength sets the scale of defocus and CTF terms.

equations.name: Contrast transfer function
equations.formula: CTF(k) = −[√(1−A²) sin χ(k) + A cos χ(k)] · E(k),  χ(k) = π λ Δf k² − (π/2) Cs λ³ k⁴
equations.meaning: A is the amplitude-contrast fraction (~0.07-0.1 for ice), Δf the defocus, k the spatial frequency and E(k) an envelope from coherence and drift. Thon rings in the power spectrum are its zeros.

equations.name: B-factor signal decay
equations.meaning: Structure-factor amplitudes fall with spatial frequency k = 1/d; sharpening applies the inverse with a negative B.

equations.name: Rosenthal-Henderson particle number
equations.meaning: The number of particles N needed to reach resolution d grows exponentially with 1/d²; the slope of a plot of ln N against 1/d² gives B.

equations.name: Fourier shell correlation
equations.meaning: Correlation between independent half-maps in each resolution shell; the gold-standard resolution is read at FSC = 0.143.

equations.name: Nyquist limit
equations.meaning: A pixel size of 0.83 Å gives Nyquist at 1.66 Å; collect at ~1/3 to 1/2 of target resolution in Å per pixel.

key_numbers.value: just thicker than the particle, ~20-60 nm

strengths: No crystals needed; works on membrane proteins in detergent or nanodiscs and on large flexible assemblies.
Captures multiple conformational and compositional states from one sample.
Requires small amounts of protein (microlitres at ~0.1-5 mg/mL).
Routine 2-4 Å maps allow de novo atomic model building and ligand identification.
limitations: Small proteins (< ~50-100 kDa) give too little signal per particle to align.
Air-water interface denaturation and preferred orientation are frequent and sample-specific.
Heterogeneous or flexible regions are blurred in the consensus map.
Instruments are expensive (300 kV microscopes cost millions) and data sets are terabytes.
best_for: Structures of membrane proteins, ion channels, transporters and receptors.
Large complexes and machines (ribosomes, spliceosome, proteasome, viruses).
Ligand and drug binding, including structure-based drug design on targets that do not crystallise.
Conformational landscapes from 3D classification and variability analysis.
sample_prep: Monodisperse, pure protein (check by size-exclusion chromatography and negative stain) is applied as 3-4 µL to a glow-discharged holey carbon or gold grid (Quantifoil, C-flat, UltrAuFoil), blotted with filter paper for a few seconds at ~95-100% humidity and 4-22 °C, then plunged into liquid ethane (Vitrobot, Leica GP) and stored under liquid nitrogen. Optimise concentration, blot time, detergent and additives; use graphene oxide or thin carbon supports, fluorinated detergents, or time-resolved sprayers to mitigate air-water interface problems.
tips: Screen grids before long collections: check ice thickness across squares (energy-filter log-ratio or a brightness atlas) and particle distribution.
Aim for ice just thick enough to embed the particle; thick ice lowers contrast through inelastic scattering, thin ice excludes or denatures particles.
If particles adopt one orientation, try tilted collection (30-40°), detergents, other supports, or different blotting.
Match pixel size to target resolution and keep dose per frame ~1 e⁻/Å²; record gain references and check for detector defects.
Keep the cryo-chain clean: frost and crystalline ice contamination appear as dark blobs and sharp diffraction spots.
Use half-map validation, local resolution and model-map FSC; never interpret features beyond the local resolution.
pitfalls: Overfitting and model bias: noise aligned to a reference can reproduce the reference ('Einstein from noise'); use gold-standard refinement and independent initial models.
Preferred orientation: anisotropic resolution and smeared density in one direction, seen in angular distribution plots and 3D FSC.
Over-masking and over-sharpening: inflated FSC and noisy, spiky maps.
Crystalline ice (hexagonal or cubic) giving rings in the power spectrum and poor contrast.
Wrong handedness: an incorrect hand gives left-handed α-helices in the map.

quiz.q: What does the CTF do to a cryo-EM image and how do you correct it?
quiz.a: The CTF modulates each spatial frequency by an oscillating sine whose zeros depend on defocus and Cs, flipping contrast in alternate bands and losing information at the zeros. Defocus is estimated from Thon rings per micrograph or per particle, and correction is done by phase flipping or Wiener-type weighting during reconstruction. Collecting over a defocus range fills the zeros.

quiz.q: Why is 0.143 used as the FSC threshold?
quiz.a: Rosenthal and Henderson showed that FSC = 0.143 between two independent half-maps corresponds to a correlation of 0.5 between the full map and a perfect reference, the conventional resolution criterion in crystallography. It only holds if the half-maps are truly independent (gold-standard refinement).

quiz.q: Your particles all show the same view. What can you do?
quiz.a: Tilt the stage during collection, change the support (graphene oxide, thin carbon), add detergents such as fluorinated octyl maltoside or CHAPSO to block the air-water interface, change blotting or use fast plunging devices, or add a binding partner that changes surface properties.

quiz.q: How do you judge ice quality during screening?
quiz.a: From the atlas brightness and energy-filter log ratio (t/λ = ln(I₀/I_zero-loss)), the power spectrum (Thon rings to high resolution without ice rings), visible particle contrast, and absence of crystalline ice or contamination.

quiz.q: What is a B-factor in cryo-EM?
quiz.a: A Gaussian fall-off term exp(−Bk²/4) summarising how signal decays with resolution due to beam-induced motion, radiation damage, alignment errors and flexibility. A lower B-factor means fewer particles are needed for a given resolution; it is also used to sharpen maps.

tagline: A frozen-hydrated cell or lamella is tilted in the electron beam and the resulting tilt series is back-projected into a 3D tomogram, revealing macromolecules in their native cellular context.
principle: Cryo-electron tomography records projection images of a vitrified specimen over a tilt range of typically ±60° in 2-3° steps. Each projection is a central section of the 3D Fourier transform (projection-slice theorem); combining them after alignment gives a 3D reconstruction by weighted back-projection or iterative methods (SIRT, SART).

Resolution depends on angular sampling: the Crowther criterion states that a specimen of thickness or diameter D reconstructed from N evenly spaced projections has resolution d ≈ π D / N. A 200 nm lamella imaged with 41 projections gives d ≈ 15 nm in the raw tomogram; higher resolution comes from subtomogram averaging of repeated structures.

Because the stage cannot tilt to 90° and the effective thickness increases as t / cos θ, a wedge of Fourier space is unsampled. This missing wedge elongates features along the beam direction (z) by a factor of about 1.55 for ±60° and smears membranes parallel to the beam. Dual-axis tilting reduces it to a missing pyramid.

The total dose (about 100-180 e⁻/Å² for the whole series) must be shared among all tilts, so each image has very low SNR. Dose-symmetric schemes (start at 0°, then alternate ±) record the most informative low-tilt images first while damage is lowest. Images are aligned with gold fiducials or by patch tracking, then CTF-corrected per tilt.

Cells thicker than ~300-500 nm are opaque to 300 kV electrons, so they are thinned by cryo-focused-ion-beam (FIB) milling to 100-250 nm lamellae. Subtomogram averaging aligns many copies of a complex in the tomograms, filling the missing wedge with different orientations and reaching sub-nanometre or even ~3-4 Å resolution for ribosomes in situ.
light_path: Field emission gun at 200-300 kV with low-dose illumination.
Specimen on a cryo-holder or autoloader cartridge: vitrified cells on grids, or FIB-milled lamellae.
Goniometer tilts the specimen in steps (e.g. 3° from −60° to +60°), with tracking and autofocus at each tilt (SerialEM, Tomo).
Objective lens images at a few micrometres under-focus; optional phase plate.
Energy filter removes inelastically scattered electrons, important because the path through tilted specimens is long.
Direct electron detector records a short dose-fractionated movie at each tilt.
Tilt series is motion-corrected, aligned, CTF-corrected and reconstructed into a 3D tomogram (IMOD, AreTomo, Warp).

resolution.xy: ~2-5 nm in raw tomograms; ~3-10 Å after subtomogram averaging
resolution.z: worse than xy by ~1.5-2 because of the missing wedge
resolution.why: Crowther angular sampling, missing wedge, specimen thickness, total dose shared over the tilt series, alignment accuracy and molecular crowding.

equations.name: Crowther criterion
equations.meaning: Resolution d achievable from N equally spaced projections of an object of diameter or thickness D; equivalently N = π D / d projections are needed.

equations.name: Missing-wedge elongation
equations.formula: e_xz = √((α + sin α cos α) / (α − sin α cos α))
equations.meaning: Elongation along z for a maximum tilt α (radians); for ±60° e ≈ 1.55, for ±70° e ≈ 1.3.

equations.name: Sampled fraction of Fourier space
equations.meaning: For ±60° single-axis tilting, two thirds of Fourier space is sampled and one third is missing.

equations.name: Effective thickness at tilt
equations.meaning: At 60° a lamella is twice as thick to the beam, so high tilts are noisier.

equations.name: Ice thickness from energy filtering
equations.meaning: Measures specimen thickness in units of the inelastic mean free path (~300-400 nm at 300 kV).

strengths: Images macromolecules inside intact, unfixed, unstained cells at molecular resolution.
Reveals spatial relationships, membrane contacts and native architecture.
Subtomogram averaging gives in situ structures of complexes that cannot be purified.
Combines with cryo-CLEM and cryo-FIB for targeted imaging of rare events.
limitations: Low throughput: a lamella takes hours to prepare and gives a few tomograms.
Missing wedge and low SNR make interpretation of raw tomograms difficult.
Thickness limits: whole-cell imaging only for the thin periphery of cells or bacteria.
Identifying molecules without averaging is hard; template matching requires known structures.
best_for: Native architecture of organelles, cytoskeleton, synapses and membrane contact sites.
In situ structures of ribosomes, nuclear pores, viruses and filament assemblies.
Bacterial and archaeal cell biology (thin cells).
Viral replication compartments and host-pathogen interfaces.
sample_prep: Cells are grown or deposited on EM grids (gold grids with holey carbon or SiO₂ films for culture) and plunge-frozen; thick samples (tissue, organisms) are high-pressure frozen. Specimens thicker than ~300 nm are thinned by cryo-FIB milling (gallium or plasma beams) into lamellae, often after cryo-fluorescence targeting, and protected with an organometallic platinum layer. Lift-out techniques extract lamellae from high-pressure frozen tissue. 10 nm gold fiducials can be added before freezing for alignment.
tips: Use dose-symmetric tilt schemes when subtomogram averaging is planned; record the zero-degree image early while the sample is undamaged.
Pre-tilt lamellae (often ~10°) so that the milling angle is compensated and the tilt range is symmetric about the lamella plane.
Monitor lamella thickness by energy-filter log-ratio; aim for 150-200 nm for cell biology and thinner for high-resolution averaging.
Keep tilt-series tracking tight; large image shifts between tilts cost dose and alignment accuracy.
Use denoising (cryo-CARE, Topaz) and missing-wedge correction (IsoNet) for visualisation, but quantify and average from raw data.
pitfalls: Missing-wedge artefacts: elongation in z and loss of membranes oriented perpendicular to the tilt axis; do not interpret absent features as absent structures.
Curtaining: stripes from uneven FIB milling across materials of different density.
Ice contamination and redeposition on lamellae during transfer, seen as dark dots and crystals.
Over-interpretation of template-matching hits; check against shuffled or mirrored templates and false-positive rates.
Beam-induced motion and charging at high tilt causing alignment residuals and blurred reconstructions.

quiz.q: State the Crowther criterion and apply it.
quiz.a: d = π D / N. For a 200 nm thick lamella and 41 projections, d ≈ 3.14 × 200 / 41 ≈ 15 nm in the raw tomogram. To reach 5 nm you would need ~125 projections, which the dose budget does not allow, so higher resolution comes from subtomogram averaging.

quiz.q: What is the missing wedge and how does it show up?
quiz.a: Because tilting is limited to about ±60°, a wedge of Fourier space around the beam axis is never measured. Objects are elongated in z (~1.55× at ±60°) and features such as membranes perpendicular to the tilt axis and parallel to the beam can disappear. Dual-axis tomography, averaging of differently oriented copies, or deep-learning correction mitigate it.

quiz.q: Why do we need cryo-FIB milling?
quiz.a: Electrons at 300 kV cannot usefully penetrate more than ~300-500 nm of ice because of multiple and inelastic scattering; most eukaryotic cells are several micrometres thick. FIB milling removes material above and below a target region to leave a 100-250 nm lamella without the compression artefacts of cryo-sectioning.

quiz.q: How would you find a rare event inside a cell for cryo-ET?
quiz.a: Use cryo-CLEM: image fluorescent markers by cryo-fluorescence (possibly in an integrated FIB), correlate to the SEM/FIB view using fiducials, mill a lamella at the target, and correlate again on the lamella before tilt-series acquisition.

tagline: Repeatedly removing a thin layer from a stained resin block and imaging the new surface, or imaging long series of sections, builds nanometre-resolution 3D volumes of cells and tissues.
principle: Volume EM (vEM) extends ultrastructure into three dimensions over volumes from a single cell to cubic millimetres of tissue. All variants combine heavy-metal staining of the whole block with serial removal or serial sectioning and electron imaging, then register the images into a stack for segmentation.

Serial block-face SEM (SBF-SEM) places an ultramicrotome inside the SEM chamber: a diamond knife cuts 25-70 nm off the block face and the freshly exposed face is imaged with backscattered electrons. Focused ion beam SEM (FIB-SEM) instead mills away 3-10 nm slices with a gallium (or plasma) beam, giving isotropic voxels down to ~4 nm, at the cost of smaller fields of view and slower volume rates.

Section-based methods keep the sections: serial-section TEM (ssTEM) and serial-section tomography image ribbons of sections on grids, while array tomography and ATUM (automated tape-collecting ultramicrotome) collect hundreds to thousands of sections on wafers or tape for SEM imaging. Sections can be re-imaged at different resolutions and with immunolabelling, and multi-beam SEMs (61 or more beams) give very high throughput.

Image contrast is BSE signal from heavy metals. Blocks must be stained very heavily and uniformly throughout (for example rOTO: reduced osmium, thiocarbohydrazide, osmium; then uranyl acetate and Walton's lead aspartate) both for contrast and to make the resin conductive, because charging at the block face is a major problem in SBF-SEM.

Resolution is anisotropic for physical sectioning (xy set by pixel size and probe, z by cut thickness) but can be isotropic for FIB-SEM. The data volumes are enormous (a cubic millimetre at 4 × 4 × 40 nm is ~1.5 × 10¹⁵ voxels), so segmentation with machine learning and proofreading is now the rate-limiting step.
light_path: Sample is heavy-metal stained en bloc, resin embedded, trimmed and mounted on a conductive pin.
SEM column forms a low-kV (1.5-3 kV) electron probe to limit the interaction volume and information depth.
BSE detector (or in-column detector) collects the backscattered signal from the block face or section.
Material removal: in SBF-SEM an in-chamber diamond knife cuts a slice; in FIB-SEM a gallium or xenon ion beam at 52-54° to the electron beam mills a slice.
Imaging and removal alternate automatically for hundreds to tens of thousands of cycles.
For array tomography or ATUM, sections are first collected on wafers or tape and imaged later, potentially with multi-beam SEM.
Images are aligned, stitched and assembled into 3D volumes for segmentation.

resolution.why: BSE information depth and probe size in xy; knife-cut thickness or ion-milling step in z; charging, beam damage of resin and stain penetration.

equations.name: Voxel count
equations.meaning: 1 mm³ at 4 × 4 × 40 nm gives ~1.6 × 10¹⁵ voxels, ~1.5 PB at 8 bits; drives acquisition time and storage.

equations.name: Acquisition time
equations.meaning: At 100 ns dwell a single-beam SEM needs ~5 years for 1.6 × 10¹⁵ voxels, which is why multi-beam SEM and parallel instruments exist.

equations.name: Kanaya-Okayama range
equations.meaning: BSE information depth scales with interaction depth; using ~1.5-2 kV keeps it to a few tens of nanometres so the effective z resolution approaches the cut thickness.

equations.name: Nyquist for membranes
equations.meaning: To trace membranes or synaptic vesicles (~40 nm) and thin axons (~100 nm), pixel size must be at most half the smallest feature width.

key_numbers.label: FIB-SEM typical volume
key_numbers.value: ~10-100 µm per side (larger with enhanced systems)

strengths: Nanometre-resolution 3D ultrastructure over cell and tissue volumes.
Unbiased, complete sampling: every synapse, organelle and contact in the volume.
Connectomics: complete wiring diagrams of neural circuits.
Combines with CLEM to find rare cells or structures.
limitations: Destructive (block-face methods) and slow; big volumes take weeks to months.
Fixed, heavily stained material only; no molecular identity without CLEM or labelling.
Huge data and segmentation burden; proofreading often dominates cost.
Anisotropic resolution for physical sectioning complicates 3D tracing.
best_for: Connectomics and synapse-level circuit reconstruction.
Organelle morphometry and contacts (mitochondria, ER, lipid droplets) in whole cells.
Tissue architecture: kidney podocytes, tumour microenvironment, plant tissues.
Host-pathogen interactions in 3D and rare events targeted by fluorescence.
sample_prep: Perfusion or immersion fixation (glutaraldehyde-paraformaldehyde) or high-pressure freezing, then intense en bloc staining (e.g. potassium ferrocyanide-reduced osmium, thiocarbohydrazide, osmium, uranyl acetate, Walton's lead aspartate), dehydration and embedding in a hard epoxy (Durcupan, hard Epon), sometimes with conductive fillers. Blocks are trimmed to a small mesa (often < 1 mm), mounted with conductive epoxy or silver paint and sputter coated on the sides. For FIB-SEM, a protective platinum or carbon pad is deposited and trenches are milled to expose the imaging face.
tips: Test stain penetration on a pilot block: the core of large tissue pieces is often under-stained.
Use focal charge compensation (a nitrogen jet), variable pressure or conductive resin to suppress charging in SBF-SEM.
Choose the cut thickness relative to the smallest structure you must trace; thin axons need ~30 nm or less.
Match dose to resin tolerance: too much dose causes the block to soften and the next cut to be thinner or skip ('chatter').
Plan data management up front: storage, chunked formats (N5, Zarr), and pipeline tools (e.g. CATMAID, webKnossos, Neuroglancer).
Include a CLEM landmark (vasculature, nuclei, near-infrared branding) to relocate the region of interest.
pitfalls: Charging: drift, bright halos and distorted block faces, especially over empty resin areas such as vessel lumens.
Missed or uneven cuts: thickness variations, double cuts or skipped slices that cause jumps in the stack.
Curtaining in FIB-SEM from uneven milling of different materials.
Extraction and swelling artefacts from chemical fixation; extracellular space shrinks unless cryo-fixation or special protocols are used.
Segmentation errors (merges and splits) propagating into wrong biological conclusions without proofreading.

quiz.q: How do you choose between SBF-SEM, FIB-SEM and array tomography?
quiz.a: SBF-SEM for large fields (hundreds of micrometres) with ~30-70 nm z steps, e.g. tissue overviews and neuron tracing. FIB-SEM for isotropic ~5-10 nm voxels over smaller volumes, e.g. organelle contacts in single cells. Array tomography or ATUM when sections must be kept for re-imaging, immunolabelling or multi-beam throughput.

quiz.q: Why is staining so different for volume EM compared with conventional TEM?
quiz.a: There is no post-staining of sections; contrast must come from en bloc heavy metals throughout the block, and the block must conduct to avoid charging at the face. Protocols such as rOTO with uranyl and lead aspartate add much more metal than standard TEM protocols.

quiz.q: Estimate the storage needed for 100 µm³ cubed at 8 nm isotropic.
quiz.a: (100 µm / 8 nm)³ = 12,500³ ≈ 2 × 10¹² voxels, i.e. ~2 TB at 8 bits before compression and pyramids.

quiz.q: What limits z resolution in SBF-SEM?
quiz.a: The reliable minimum cut thickness (~25 nm, set by resin hardness and beam damage) and the BSE information depth, which is why low landing energies are used.

tagline: A nanometre-sharp tip on a flexible cantilever is scanned over a surface, and the cantilever deflection maps topography and mechanical properties with sub-nanometre height precision in liquid.
principle: An atomic force microscope senses the force between a sharp tip and the sample rather than forming an image with waves. The tip sits at the end of a microfabricated cantilever that behaves as a spring obeying Hooke's law; a laser reflected off its back onto a quadrant photodiode (optical lever) measures deflections down to ~0.1 nm.

In contact mode the feedback keeps deflection (force) constant while a piezo scanner rasters the sample, and the z-piezo signal gives height. In intermittent-contact (tapping, AC) mode the cantilever oscillates near its resonance frequency and feedback holds the amplitude constant; lateral forces are reduced, which is essential for soft biological samples. Off-resonance modes such as PeakForce tapping record a force curve at every pixel and give quantitative mechanical maps.

Force spectroscopy measures force versus distance at a single point: approach curves are fitted with contact mechanics (Hertz or Sneddon models) to get Young's modulus, retraction curves show adhesion, and single-molecule pulling reveals protein unfolding as sawtooth peaks described by worm-like chain elasticity.

Lateral resolution is set by the tip apex radius (typically 2-20 nm) and by tip-sample convolution: features smaller than the tip appear broadened, and steep sidewalls are imaged with the tip's own shape. Vertical resolution is limited by thermal noise and feedback, typically ~0.1 nm.

AFM works in physiological buffer and does not need labels. High-speed AFM with small cantilevers (resonances in the MHz range in liquid) and fast feedback reaches 10-20 frames per second, allowing movies of single proteins such as myosin V walking on actin.
light_path: Probe: a silicon or silicon nitride cantilever (tens to hundreds of µm long) with a sharp tip of radius ~2-20 nm.
Detection laser is focused on the back of the cantilever.
Reflected beam lands on a four-segment photodiode; the vertical difference signal reports bending, the lateral difference reports torsion (friction).
Feedback controller compares the deflection or amplitude signal with a setpoint.
Piezo scanner moves the sample or tip in x, y (raster) and z (feedback), with closed-loop sensors for linearity.
Height, error (deflection or amplitude), phase and force-curve channels are recorded at each pixel.

resolution.xy: ~1-20 nm on biological samples (sub-nm on flat crystals and membranes)
resolution.why: Tip radius and tip convolution, sample softness and deformation, thermal noise of the cantilever, and feedback bandwidth.

equations.name: Hooke's law
equations.meaning: Force on the tip equals cantilever spring constant k times its deflection Δz; e.g. 0.05 N/m × 1 nm = 50 pN.

equations.name: Cantilever resonance
equations.meaning: Stiffer, lighter cantilevers resonate at higher frequency; resonance drops several-fold in liquid due to added hydrodynamic mass.

equations.name: Thermal (equipartition) calibration
equations.meaning: The mean-square thermal fluctuation of the free cantilever gives its spring constant (Hutter and Bechhoefer), with a mode-shape correction factor in practice.

equations.name: Hertz model for a spherical indenter
equations.meaning: Relates indentation δ to force F for tip radius R, sample Young's modulus E and Poisson ratio ν (~0.5 for cells).

equations.name: Tip convolution of a sphere
equations.meaning: A tip of radius R imaging a sphere or rod of radius r gives apparent width w; a 2 nm DNA strand (r = 1 nm) under a 10 nm tip appears ~13 nm wide, while its height remains accurate.

equations.name: Worm-like chain
equations.meaning: Force-extension of a polymer with persistence length p and contour length L, used to fit single-molecule unfolding peaks.

key_numbers.label: Soft cantilever spring constant
key_numbers.value: ~0.01-0.1 N/m for cells and contact imaging

key_numbers.label: Thermal force noise
key_numbers.value: ~ pN in a ~kHz bandwidth with soft cantilevers

key_numbers.label: Typical scan size
key_numbers.value: up to ~100 µm, z range ~5-15 µm

strengths: Label-free imaging in physiological buffer, from single molecules to living cells.
Sub-nanometre height precision and true 3D topography.
Directly measures forces and mechanics: stiffness, adhesion, single-molecule unfolding.
Combines with fluorescence on inverted microscopes.
limitations: Surface only; cannot see inside cells.
Slow conventional scanning (minutes per image) and small scan ranges.
Tip convolution broadens lateral features; soft samples deform under the tip.
Tips wear and contaminate; quantitative mechanics depend on careful calibration and model choice.
best_for: Structure and dynamics of membrane proteins, DNA-protein complexes and amyloid fibrils on flat supports.
Cell and tissue mechanics (stiffness maps, mechanobiology, cancer and fibrosis).
Single-molecule force spectroscopy of protein unfolding and ligand-receptor binding.
Surface characterisation of biomaterials, lipid bilayers and nanoparticles.
sample_prep: Samples must be firmly immobilised on a flat support: freshly cleaved mica (often with Mg²⁺ or Ni²⁺ for DNA, APTES for proteins), glass or supported lipid bilayers. Cells are imaged in culture dishes in buffer at controlled temperature. Proteins are adsorbed at low density. Avoid loosely attached material, which the tip drags. For mechanics, choose tip geometry (sharp pyramid vs colloidal sphere) to match the scale of interest.
tips: Calibrate deflection sensitivity on a hard surface (glass) in the same liquid, then calibrate spring constant by the thermal method.
Use the lowest force (setpoint) that keeps tracking; check trace and retrace lines overlap.
Let the system thermally equilibrate in liquid for 20-30 min to reduce drift.
For cells use soft cantilevers (k ~0.01-0.1 N/m), slow scan rates and moderate indentation depths (< ~10% of cell height) for Hertz fitting.
Image a calibration grating and a sharp-tip characteriser to check scanner calibration and tip shape.
Replace the tip if images show repeating double features or sudden resolution loss.
pitfalls: Tip convolution: features appear wider than they are; use heights for size estimates.
Double or triple tip artefacts: every feature repeated with the same offset, from a broken or contaminated tip.
Sample deformation: soft molecules look lower than their true height at high force.
Piezo creep and hysteresis, thermal drift: distorted, sheared or stretched images.
Wrong contact model or substrate effect: overestimated stiffness on thin samples (bottom effect).

quiz.q: Why does DNA look 10-20 nm wide in AFM when it is 2 nm across?
quiz.a: Tip convolution: the measured width is roughly 4√(Rr) for tip radius R and object radius r, so a ~10 nm tip broadens it strongly. Heights are accurate (though slightly reduced by compression), so use height rather than width for size.

quiz.q: How do you measure cell stiffness by AFM and what are the caveats?
quiz.a: Record force-indentation curves with a calibrated soft cantilever, then fit a Hertz or Sneddon model with the correct tip geometry and Poisson ratio. Caveats: calibration of sensitivity and k, contact point detection, indentation depth relative to cell height (substrate effect), viscoelasticity and loading rate, and position over nucleus vs periphery.

quiz.q: Contact versus tapping mode for biological samples?
quiz.a: Contact mode applies constant normal and significant lateral forces that can sweep or damage soft samples; tapping or off-resonance modes touch the surface intermittently, minimising lateral forces, and are preferred for single molecules and cells. Contact mode can work well on flat, tightly packed membranes such as 2D crystals.

quiz.q: How do you calibrate an AFM cantilever?
quiz.a: First measure deflection sensitivity (nm per volt) from the slope of a force curve on a hard surface; then measure thermal fluctuations of the free cantilever and use equipartition, k = k_BT/⟨Δz²⟩ with a mode correction (or the Sader method from resonance and Q).

tagline: X-rays penetrate millimetres to centimetres of tissue, so rotating a sample in the beam and reconstructing the projections gives 3D images from whole organisms (micro-CT) down to frozen single cells (soft X-ray tomography).
principle: X-ray imaging contrast comes mainly from absorption, which follows the Beer-Lambert law. The linear attenuation coefficient μ depends on electron density and atomic number and falls steeply with energy (photoelectric absorption scales roughly as Z³-Z⁴/E³), so bone, calcium deposits and heavy-metal stains absorb strongly while soft tissue is nearly transparent at hard X-ray energies.

Micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) records radiographs while rotating the sample through 180-360° and reconstructs a 3D volume by filtered back-projection, exactly as in clinical CT but with micrometre voxels. Laboratory systems use microfocus tubes (20-160 kV) and achieve ~1-50 µm voxels; synchrotron and nano-CT reach ~50 nm-1 µm. Soft tissues need contrast agents such as iodine (Lugol's solution), phosphotungstic acid (PTA) or osmium.

Phase contrast exploits the refractive index decrement δ, which for soft tissue at hard X-ray energies is roughly 1000 times larger than the absorption index β. Propagation-based (in-line) phase contrast, grating interferometry and phase retrieval make soft tissue visible without stain, especially with coherent synchrotron beams.

Soft X-ray microscopy works in the 'water window' between the carbon K edge (284 eV, 4.37 nm) and the oxygen K edge (543 eV, 2.34 nm). Here carbon-rich material (proteins, lipids) absorbs about an order of magnitude more than water, giving natural contrast in unstained, vitrified whole cells up to ~10 µm thick. Images are formed with Fresnel zone plates whose resolution is set by the outermost zone width; soft X-ray tomography (cryo-SXT) gives ~25-50 nm 3D maps of whole cells.

Radiation dose is the central trade-off: better resolution requires more photons per voxel, and dose rises roughly as the inverse fourth power of the voxel size for constant signal-to-noise. Cryo-cooling greatly reduces the visible damage in soft X-ray work.
light_path: Source: microfocus X-ray tube (laboratory micro-CT), synchrotron undulator or bending magnet (nano-CT, phase contrast, soft X-ray), or a laser-plasma source.
Optional filtering and monochromatisation (metal filters on lab sources harden the spectrum; monochromators at synchrotrons).
Condenser (capillary or zone plate) for full-field X-ray microscopes; cone beam geometry for lab micro-CT.
Sample on a high-precision rotation stage, often in a sealed tube or cryo-stage.
Objective zone plate (X-ray microscopes) or geometric magnification by source-sample-detector distances (cone-beam CT).
Detector: scintillator imaged by optics onto a CCD/CMOS, or direct photon-counting detectors; for soft X-rays a back-illuminated CCD.
Projections over a range of angles are reconstructed by filtered back-projection or iterative algorithms.

resolution.xy: micro-CT ~1-50 µm; nano-CT ~50-500 nm; soft X-ray tomography ~25-50 nm
resolution.z: isotropic for full-rotation CT; anisotropic for limited-tilt soft X-ray tomography
resolution.why: Source spot size and detector pixel (geometric magnification), zone plate outermost width, angular sampling, photon count and radiation dose, and sample motion.

equations.name: Beer-Lambert attenuation
equations.meaning: Transmitted intensity through thickness x of material with linear attenuation coefficient μ; CT reconstructs μ(x, y, z).

equations.name: Photoelectric scaling
equations.meaning: Mass attenuation rises steeply with atomic number and falls with photon energy, explaining bone and heavy-stain contrast and the use of low energies for soft tissue.

equations.name: Hounsfield units
equations.meaning: Normalised CT number: water = 0, air = −1000, bone several hundred to >1000.

equations.name: Complex refractive index
equations.meaning: δ gives phase shift, β absorption; for soft tissue at ~20 keV δ/β ~ 10³, which is why phase contrast is so much more sensitive.

equations.name: Zone plate resolution
equations.meaning: Rayleigh resolution of a Fresnel zone plate with outermost zone width Δr_N; 25 nm zones give ~30 nm resolution.

equations.name: Geometric magnification (cone beam)
equations.meaning: Moving the sample closer to the source magnifies it, but blur from the source spot size grows as (M − 1) × spot size.

key_numbers.label: Soft X-ray tomography resolution
key_numbers.value: ~25-50 nm, cells up to ~10-15 µm thick

strengths: Large penetration: whole organs, embryos, insects and biopsies imaged in 3D without sectioning.
Non-destructive, so samples can be imaged and then sectioned for histology or EM.
Isotropic 3D volumes with quantitative density (bone mineral density, porosity).
Soft X-ray tomography images whole, unstained, frozen cells at tens of nanometres.
limitations: Poor intrinsic soft-tissue contrast with absorption; staining or phase contrast needed.
Radiation dose limits resolution in living or hydrated samples.
Highest resolutions require synchrotron access.
No molecular specificity without labels or correlative fluorescence.
best_for: Bone and tooth morphology, mineral density and implant integration.
Embryo and small-animal phenotyping (iodine or PTA-stained mouse embryos, zebrafish, insects).
Navigating large samples before volume EM (finding a region in a resin block).
Whole-cell organelle morphometry by cryo-SXT (mitochondria, lipid droplets, nuclear architecture).
sample_prep: Micro-CT of mineralised tissue needs little preparation beyond fixation and stable mounting. Soft tissue is fixed and stained with contrast agents (Lugol's iodine, PTA, phosphomolybdic acid, osmium) for hours to weeks depending on size, or imaged unstained with phase contrast. Samples are immobilised in tubes (agarose, ethanol, or embedded in resin or paraffin) to prevent motion. Cryo-SXT uses cells loaded into glass capillaries or on grids and vitrified by plunge freezing.
tips: Choose voxel size to match the feature; the field of view is roughly the detector width in pixels times the voxel size.
Use beam filtering (aluminium or copper) to reduce beam hardening on dense samples.
Check stain penetration over time: PTA penetrates slowly and can leave unstained cores in large samples.
Let samples equilibrate and mount them rigidly; even micrometre motion during long scans blurs reconstructions.
Acquire flat-field and dark images and use rotation-centre correction during reconstruction.
pitfalls: Beam hardening: dense objects appear brighter at edges (cupping) and dark streaks run between them.
Ring artefacts from defective or miscalibrated detector pixels.
Motion and drying artefacts: doubled edges or shrinking during the scan.
Stain-induced shrinkage (iodine) or uneven penetration mistaken for biology.
Partial-volume effects at boundaries smaller than a few voxels.

history.event: Röntgen discovers X-rays.
Kirkpatrick and Baez propose grazing-incidence mirror optics for focusing X-rays.
Hounsfield describes computerised transverse axial tomography (Nobel Prize 1979 with Cormack).
During the 1980s zone-plate soft X-ray microscopes are developed at synchrotrons by groups in Göttingen and at Stony Brook/Brookhaven.
Larabell and Le Gros reconstruct whole yeast cells by soft X-ray tomography.
Metscher shows simple contrast stains make soft tissue visible by lab micro-CT.

papers.note: The first CT system; the foundation of tomographic X-ray imaging.

papers.cite: Kirz J, Jacobsen C, Howells M (1995) Q Rev Biophys 28:33-130
papers.note: Comprehensive review of soft X-ray microscopes and biological applications.

quiz.q: Why is soft tissue hard to see by micro-CT and how do you fix it?
quiz.a: At hard X-ray energies soft tissue components have similar, low attenuation, differing mostly in density, not atomic number. Use heavy-element contrast agents (iodine, PTA, osmium), lower tube voltage, or phase-contrast imaging, which exploits the much larger refractive index decrement.

quiz.q: What is the water window?
quiz.a: The soft X-ray range between the carbon K edge (284 eV) and oxygen K edge (543 eV) where water is relatively transparent but carbon-containing biomolecules absorb strongly, giving natural contrast for unstained, frozen cells.

quiz.q: What is beam hardening?
quiz.a: Polychromatic lab beams lose low-energy photons preferentially as they pass through the sample, so the mean energy rises with path length and the effective μ falls. Reconstruction then shows cupping and streaks. Mitigate with filters, lower-density mounting, or beam-hardening correction.

quiz.q: How would you use micro-CT in a volume EM workflow?
quiz.a: Scan the stained resin block to locate the target (a cell, a lesion, a vessel branch) in 3D, then use the coordinates to trim and orient the block before SBF-SEM or FIB-SEM.

tagline: Correlative light and electron microscopy combines the molecular specificity and live dynamics of fluorescence with the ultrastructural context and resolution of electron microscopy on the same sample.
principle: Fluorescence can show which molecule is where and when, including in living cells, but only at ~200 nm resolution and without context: unlabelled structures are invisible. EM shows everything at nanometre resolution but cannot easily say which protein is which. CLEM images the same cell or region with both and overlays them.

The key technical problem is registration: finding the same location in two images that differ by ~100-1000× in resolution, contrast mechanism and often sample state. Landmarks (finder grids, cell shapes, nuclei) give coarse correlation; fiducials visible in both modalities (fluorescent beads containing gold or dense material, quantum dots) give fine correlation, with fitted precision of tens of nanometres when enough fiducials surround the target.

Workflows differ by when light imaging happens. In pre-embedding CLEM, live or fixed fluorescence is recorded first and the sample is then processed for EM, so the fluorescence-EM mapping must survive fixation, staining and sectioning distortions. In in-resin CLEM, high-pressure freezing and freeze substitution with low uranyl acetate in Lowicryl HM20 preserve fluorescent protein signal in sections, so the same section is imaged by both modalities. In cryo-CLEM, vitrified samples are imaged by cryo-fluorescence and then by cryo-FIB/cryo-ET.

Genetically encoded EM tags provide molecular identity directly in the EM. APEX2 (an engineered peroxidase) and miniSOG (a flavin-binding singlet-oxygen generator) polymerise diaminobenzidine (DAB) locally, which is then stained with osmium and becomes electron dense. Other tags include ferritin, metallothionein and nanobodies coupled to gold.
Integrated systems put a light microscope inside the EM or FIB-SEM chamber, so fluorescence and EM images are inherently registered, reducing transfer and relocation steps.
light_path: Fluorescence acquisition: live-cell or fixed-cell widefield, confocal or super-resolution imaging, often on gridded coverslips or finder grids.
Fixation (chemical or high-pressure freezing) at a defined time after an observed event.
Processing for EM: staining, dehydration, resin embedding (or vitrification for cryo-CLEM).
Relocation: finder-grid coordinates, laser branding (NIRB) or micro-CT locate the region.
EM imaging: TEM of sections, electron tomography, SBF-SEM or FIB-SEM volumes, or cryo-ET of lamellae.
Registration: fiducial-based affine or non-rigid transformation maps the fluorescence onto the EM image; precision estimated by leave-one-out prediction of fiducials.

resolution.xy: EM resolution for structure; correlation precision ~10-100 nm (fiducial based) to µm (landmark based)
resolution.z: set by EM method (section thickness or tomography) and fluorescence z resolution (~500-800 nm confocal)
resolution.why: Fluorescence resolution and localisation precision, fiducial density, sample deformation between modalities, and z mismatch between optical sections and physical sections.

equations.name: Affine registration
equations.meaning: A 2×2 (or 3×3) matrix A plus translation t maps fluorescence to EM coordinates, fitted by least squares from ≥3 (2D) or ≥4 (3D) non-collinear fiducial pairs.

equations.name: Target registration error
equations.meaning: Error at the target grows with fiducial localisation error FLE and distance from the fiducial centroid, and shrinks with the number of fiducials N; K is the number of dimensions, d_k the target distance from the fiducial centroid along principal axis k and f_k the RMS fiducial spread along that axis (Fitzpatrick); surround the target with fiducials.

equations.name: Localisation precision
equations.meaning: Fiducial centres in fluorescence can be found far more precisely than the diffraction limit s if they are bright.

equations.name: Resolution gap
equations.meaning: One fluorescent spot covers hundreds of EM pixels in each direction, which is why fiducials and EM-visible tags matter.

key_numbers.label: Fiducial-based correlation accuracy
key_numbers.value: ~30-100 nm (2D in-resin), better with many fiducials

key_numbers.label: Fiducial bead size
key_numbers.value: ~50-200 nm fluorescent beads; 10-15 nm gold for tomography

key_numbers.label: Freeze-substitution uranyl acetate
key_numbers.value: ~0.1% in acetone to keep GFP fluorescent

strengths: Molecular identity plus ultrastructure on the same cell.
Captures rare, transient or live-observed events and then sees them in full context.
Targets EM to the right cell, saving enormous search time in volume EM and cryo-ET.
Validates super-resolution interpretations against EM.
limitations: Labour intensive, low throughput, many failure points.
Fluorescence often quenched by osmium and heavy-metal staining.
Sample deformation (shrinkage, section compression) complicates registration.
Z mismatch: an optical section (~600 nm) contains many EM sections.
best_for: Ultrastructure of a specific event filmed live (e.g. a fusion pore, an infection, an endocytic site).
Identifying which organelle or vesicle carries a protein.
Targeted cryo-ET of rare cellular states.
Finding a labelled neuron or cell in a large tissue volume before volume EM.
sample_prep: Grow cells on gridded glass-bottom dishes or sapphire discs with finder patterns; add fiducials (fluorescent beads, gold) where needed. For live-to-EM, fix rapidly after the event (chemical fixation within seconds or high-pressure freezing within ~1 min). For in-resin CLEM, high-pressure freeze, freeze substitute in acetone with ~0.1% uranyl acetate, embed in Lowicryl HM20 at low temperature, cut 200-300 nm sections, image fluorescence then tomography. For genetically encoded tags, express APEX2 or miniSOG fusions, fix, perform DAB reaction (with H₂O₂ or illumination), stain with osmium and process normally.
tips: Record many fluorescence overviews at increasing magnification; landmarks at all scales make relocation easy.
Use near-infrared branding or carbon markers to mark the region in tissue blocks.
Image fluorescence after fixation as well as live, because fixation can shift structures.
Quantify correlation accuracy by predicting the position of fiducials not used in the fit.
Pick fluorophores that survive the chosen protocol (mScarlet, mWasabi and mEos4 variants have been reported to survive in-resin conditions better than EGFP).
pitfalls: Mis-correlation from too few or poorly distributed fiducials, especially far from the target.
Assuming a diffraction-limited spot equals the EM structure underneath it; multiple structures lie within the same spot.
Fluorescence lost or redistributed during processing; autofluorescence of resin mistaken for signal.
Distortion from section compression or block shrinkage handled with an affine model when non-rigid registration is needed.
Event observed live may have changed during the time to fixation.

history.event: Maranto shows that illuminating a fluorescent dye (Lucifer Yellow) in the presence of DAB produces an electron-dense product, the basis of photoconversion CLEM.
Genetically encoded tetracysteine/ReAsH tags enable photoconversion CLEM (Gaietta and colleagues).
Kukulski and colleagues show high-precision in-resin CLEM with electron tomography.
Shu and colleagues introduce miniSOG as a genetically encoded CLEM tag.
Martell and colleagues introduce APEX, an engineered peroxidase EM tag (APEX2 in 2015).
Integrated light-EM and cryo-CLEM workflows become commercially available and reviewed (de Boer, Hoogenboom and Giepmans).

papers.note: In-resin fluorescence correlated with electron tomography at high sensitivity and precision.

papers.note: miniSOG, a genetically encoded tag for correlated LM and EM.

papers.note: Engineered ascorbate peroxidase (APEX) as a genetically encoded EM reporter.

papers.cite: de Boer P, Hoogenboom JP, Giepmans BNG (2015) Nat Methods 12:503-513
papers.note: Widely cited review of CLEM workflows and probes.

quiz.q: How do you achieve and verify accurate correlation between fluorescence and EM?
quiz.a: Use fiducials visible in both modalities surrounding the target, fit a transformation (affine or non-rigid) by least squares, and estimate accuracy by leave-one-out prediction of fiducials not used in the fit. Precision of tens of nanometres is achievable with in-resin CLEM and tomography.

quiz.q: Why does fluorescence disappear during EM processing and how do you keep it?
quiz.a: Osmium tetroxide, high uranyl concentrations, dehydration and epoxy polymerisation at high temperature quench fluorescent proteins. Keep it by high-pressure freezing, freeze substitution with low uranyl acetate and no osmium, and low-temperature acrylic resins such as Lowicryl HM20; alternatively image fluorescence before processing or use EM-visible tags such as APEX2.

quiz.q: What is APEX2 and when would you use it instead of fluorescence correlation?
quiz.a: An engineered peroxidase that polymerises DAB in situ; the polymer binds osmium and becomes electron dense, marking the protein directly in EM with ~nm-scale spread. Use it when you need the label in every EM section or volume without registration, e.g. in volume EM of tissue.

quiz.q: Describe a cryo-CLEM workflow for cryo-ET.
quiz.a: Grow and vitrify cells on grids, image with a cryo-fluorescence microscope to find targets, transfer to a cryo-FIB-SEM, correlate fluorescence with SEM/FIB images using fiducial beads, mill a lamella through the target, optionally confirm by fluorescence on the lamella, then collect tilt series in the TEM.

tagline: Automated microscopes image every well of 96- to 1536-well plates and image analysis turns each cell into a vector of measurements, so that thousands of genetic or chemical perturbations can be compared quantitatively.
principle: High-content screening (HCS), also called high-content imaging or analysis, combines automated widefield or spinning-disk confocal microscopes, robotic plate handling and image analysis. 'High content' refers to the many features measured per cell (intensity, morphology, texture, localisation, counts) as opposed to a single plate-reader number per well.

Each plate is a 2D array of experiments. The system moves to each well, autofocuses, acquires several fields in several channels, and moves on; a 384-well plate at 4 fields and 4 channels means ~6,000 images. Speed is limited by stage moves, autofocus, exposure and filter changes, so fast laser autofocus, multi-band filters and large-chip sCMOS cameras matter.

Autofocus is usually done with a laser reflected off the plate bottom (hardware or reflection autofocus), followed by a user-defined offset into the cells; image-based autofocus is slower but follows the sample. Plate bottoms are not flat at the micrometre scale, so every well (or field) needs focus.

Assay quality is judged statistically. The Z' factor compares the separation of positive and negative controls to their variability; Z' > 0.5 is considered an excellent assay window. Plate-level and positional effects (edge effects, row/column gradients, dispensing errors) are removed by normalisation (per-plate controls, B-score, robust z-score) and randomised layouts.

Image analysis segments nuclei (usually from a DNA stain) and then cells, extracts hundreds to thousands of features per cell, and aggregates them into well-level profiles. Unbiased morphological profiling, such as Cell Painting with six dyes in five channels, uses these profiles to cluster compounds by mechanism of action, detect toxicity and link genes to phenotypes; deep learning embeddings increasingly replace hand-crafted features.
light_path: Plate handling: a robotic arm or stacker loads the plate into an environmental chamber (37 °C, 5% CO₂ for live assays).
Light source: LED or laser lines selected per channel.
Optics: widefield epifluorescence, spinning-disk or line-scanning confocal, often with water-immersion objectives for higher NA through plastic or glass bottoms.
Laser autofocus finds the plate bottom in each well; a user offset positions the focal plane in the cells.
Emission filters (often multi-band) and one or more sCMOS cameras record each channel, sometimes simultaneously.
Stage moves to the next field and well in a serpentine pattern.
Images stream to a server for analysis (CellProfiler, Harmony, MetaXpress, Columbus, deep-learning pipelines).

resolution.z: ~1-5 µm (widefield depth of field) or ~1 µm confocal
resolution.why: Throughput favours low-magnification, moderate-NA objectives through plastic plate bottoms; NA, plate bottom thickness and autofocus accuracy limit resolution.

equations.name: Z' factor
equations.meaning: Assay quality from means μ and standard deviations σ of positive and negative controls. Z' ≥ 0.5 excellent, 0 to 0.5 marginal, < 0 unusable for single-point screening.

equations.name: Strictly standardised mean difference
equations.meaning: Effect size for hit selection that accounts for variability of both groups; widely used in RNAi screens.

equations.name: Robust z-score
equations.meaning: Per-plate normalisation insensitive to hits and outliers; MAD is the median absolute deviation.

equations.name: Throughput
equations.formula: t_plate ≈ N_wells × N_fields × (t_move + t_AF + Σ t_exposure)
equations.meaning: Plate time is dominated by moves and autofocus; e.g. 384 × 4 × (0.3 + 0.2 + 4 × 0.05 s) ≈ 18 min.

equations.name: Depth of field
equations.formula: d_z ≈ λ n / NA² + n e / (M NA)
equations.meaning: Low-NA objectives tolerate plate-bottom variation; high NA needs per-field focus.

key_numbers.label: Plate bottom
key_numbers.value: ~170-190 µm glass or cyclic olefin polymer for high NA

strengths: Quantitative, multiparametric phenotypes at single-cell resolution across thousands of conditions.
Captures heterogeneity and subpopulations lost in bulk assays.
Unbiased morphological profiling for mechanism of action and toxicity.
Automation and standardisation suit pharma pipelines and arrayed CRISPR or RNAi screens.
limitations: Usually lower resolution and simpler optics than research microscopes.
Large data volumes and complex analysis; batch effects between plates and days.
Mostly 2D cultures; 3D organoid screening is slower and harder to segment.
Hit rates depend heavily on assay design, controls and normalisation.
best_for: Phenotypic drug discovery and compound profiling.
Arrayed genome-wide RNAi or CRISPR screens.
Toxicity and cell-health assays (nuclear morphology, mitochondrial potential, cell count).
Translocation assays (e.g. NF-κB nuclear translocation), neurite outgrowth, receptor internalisation.
sample_prep: Seed cells uniformly with automated dispensers, let plates settle at room temperature for 30-60 min before moving them to the incubator to avoid edge-biased settling, treat with compounds by acoustic or pin transfer, then fix, permeabilise and stain with robotic washers (or image live). Use plates with optically flat bottoms suited to the objective (glass or cyclic olefin for high NA). Include positive and negative controls on every plate, distributed across rows and columns, and randomise or balance treatment layouts.
tips: Fill outer wells with medium or buffer, use humidified incubators and breathable seals, and pre-equilibrate plates to reduce evaporation-driven edge effects.
Spread controls across the plate rather than in a single column so that positional bias can be detected and corrected.
Validate the laser autofocus offset in several wells and plates; check for out-of-focus images with a focus metric (e.g. power log-log slope) in QC.
Avoid wash steps that detach mitotic or dying cells; low cell counts bias features.
Use flat-field (illumination) correction per channel before intensity measurements.
Run a pilot with replicate plates on different days to estimate Z', plate-to-plate variability and the number of replicates needed.
pitfalls: Edge effects: altered growth or staining in outer wells from evaporation and temperature gradients, visible as a ring pattern in plate heat maps.
Autofocus failures: whole wells out of focus, often in wells with few cells, bubbles or debris; flagged by low focus scores or segmentation counts.
Compound autofluorescence or precipitate mistaken for a phenotype.
Cytotoxicity confounding: fewer cells changes many features; always report cell count.
Batch effects across plates and days that dominate the biological signal if not normalised and randomised.

history.event: Cellomics launches the ArrayScan, an early commercial high-content screening platform.
Zhang, Chung and Oldenburg introduce the Z' factor for screening assay quality.
CellProfiler released as open-source software for high-throughput cell image analysis.
MitoCheck: genome-wide RNAi screen by live time-lapse imaging of cell division (Neumann et al.).
Cell Painting protocol published for morphological profiling.
The JUMP Cell Painting consortium releases profiles of >100,000 compounds and genetic perturbations.

papers.note: Definition of the Z' factor for assay validation.

papers.note: CellProfiler, the open-source standard for HCS image analysis.

papers.note: Genome-wide phenotypic profiling by time-lapse microscopy (MitoCheck).

papers.note: Review of microscopy-based high-content screening.
