papers.note: Cell Painting protocol for image-based morphological profiling.

quiz.q: Define the Z' factor and interpret a value of 0.3.
quiz.a: Z' = 1 − 3(σp + σn)/|μp − μn|. A value of 0.3 means the 3-sigma bands of the controls are close; the assay can detect strong hits but single-point screening will have many false positives and negatives. Improve by reducing variability (more cells per well, better normalisation, more fields) or increasing the window.

quiz.q: How do you detect and correct plate edge effects?
quiz.a: Plot per-well readouts as plate heat maps and look for row, column or ring patterns; compare controls placed at edges and centre. Prevent with humidity, room-temperature settling after seeding, outer wells filled with buffer; correct with B-score or spatial normalisation, but do not normalise away true hits.

quiz.q: Laser autofocus versus image-based autofocus?
quiz.a: Laser autofocus finds the reflection from the plate bottom quickly and independently of the sample, then applies a fixed offset; it fails if cell height or bottom thickness varies. Image-based autofocus maximises a sharpness metric on the sample itself; it is slower, needs signal and can lock onto debris. Many systems combine both.

quiz.q: What is Cell Painting and what is it used for?
quiz.a: A multiplexed stain (Hoechst, concanavalin A, SYTO 14, phalloidin plus WGA, MitoTracker) imaged in five channels to capture nuclei, ER, nucleoli/RNA, actin/Golgi/plasma membrane and mitochondria. Thousands of features per cell form a morphological profile used for mechanism-of-action clustering, toxicity and gene function annotation.

quiz.q: Why might a hit with strong phenotype be a false positive?
quiz.a: Cytotoxicity, compound autofluorescence, precipitation, focus failures, plate position, or dispensing errors. Check cell counts, raw images, replicates, dose-response and orthogonal assays.

tagline: Whole-slide scanners image entire histology slides at sub-micrometre resolution, producing gigapixel digital slides for pathology, image analysis and AI.
principle: A whole-slide imaging (WSI) system digitises a full glass slide by scanning many small fields or strips with a 20× or 40× objective and stitching them into one image. A tissue section of 15 × 15 mm at 0.25 µm per pixel gives 60,000 × 60,000 pixels (3.6 gigapixels, ~10 GB uncompressed RGB), stored as a multi-resolution pyramid so viewers can zoom like a map.

Scanners use either tile (step-and-shoot) acquisition with an area camera or line scanning with a linear or TDI (time-delay integration) sensor that moves continuously along strips. Line scanning avoids most stitching seams and is fast; TDI accumulates signal over several rows for fluorescence and low light.

Focus is the main technical challenge because sections are not flat and the depth of field at 40× (NA ~0.75) is only ~1 µm. Scanners build a focus map from points sampled across the tissue before scanning, or use real-time dynamic focus with a secondary sensor. Z-stacking or extended-focus imaging is used for thick specimens such as cytology smears.

Brightfield scanning of H&E and immunohistochemistry dominates clinical use; fluorescence and multiplex scanners image several to dozens of markers. Colour reproducibility depends on stain, scanner optics and camera, so colour calibration and stain normalisation are essential for quantitative and AI work.

Digital pathology enables remote diagnosis, archiving, education, quantitative image analysis (e.g. QuPath) and deep learning models that classify tumours or predict mutations from H&E. Primary diagnosis on WSI requires validation against glass-slide diagnosis in the laboratory's own setting, following professional guidelines and regulatory clearance.
light_path: Slide loading from racks of tens to hundreds of slides; a macro camera photographs the whole slide and label (barcode).
Tissue detection on the macro image defines the scan area.
Brightfield Köhler illumination (LED) or epifluorescence illumination for fluorescence scanners.
Objective (typically 20× NA 0.75 or 40× NA 0.95, sometimes with a 2× doubler) images the tissue.
Focus map built from sampled points, or real-time focus using an auxiliary sensor.
Line-scan, TDI or area camera captures strips or tiles while the stage moves.
Stitching, colour correction and JPEG/JPEG2000 compression produce a pyramidal file (SVS, NDPI, MRXS, or DICOM WSI).

resolution.xy: ~0.25 µm/pixel at 40× ('40×-equivalent'), ~0.5 µm/pixel at 20×; optical resolution ~0.4-0.6 µm
resolution.z: single focal plane of ~1-2 µm depth of field unless z-stacked
resolution.why: Objective NA, camera pixel sampling, focus accuracy across uneven tissue, and compression.

equations.name: Image size
equations.meaning: 15 × 15 mm at p = 0.25 µm gives 3.6 × 10⁹ pixels; halving p quadruples data.

equations.name: Nyquist sampling
equations.meaning: With NA 0.75 at 550 nm, d ≈ 0.45 µm, so pixels of ≤ ~0.22 µm are needed to fully sample the optics.

equations.name: Depth of field
equations.meaning: At NA 0.75, d_z ≈ 1 µm, comparable to section unevenness, hence the need for focus maps.

equations.name: Beer-Lambert for stains (optical density)
equations.meaning: Colour deconvolution separates haematoxylin, eosin and DAB by their optical density vectors (Ruifrok and Johnston); OD is linear in stain amount, RGB is not.

key_numbers.label: Scan time
key_numbers.value: ~30 s to a few minutes per brightfield slide

key_numbers.label: Slide capacity
key_numbers.value: up to several hundred slides per load

strengths: Entire slide digitised: no sampling bias from selected fields.
Enables telepathology, archiving, education and multi-site review.
Foundation for quantitative image analysis and AI in pathology.
High throughput with autoloaders; standard file formats (DICOM WSI).
limitations: Single focal plane at modest NA; poor for thick or uneven specimens without z-stacks.
Huge files and storage costs; proprietary formats.
Colour variation between labs and scanners complicates AI generalisation.
Some tasks (e.g. polarisation, small organisms such as H. pylori, mitoses) can be harder than on glass.
best_for: Clinical histopathology and second-opinion review.
Tissue microarray and IHC quantification (e.g. Ki-67, HER2, PD-L1).
Training and deploying deep learning models on H&E slides.
Spatial biology: multiplex immunofluorescence slide scanning.
sample_prep: Standard formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) sections at 3-5 µm, flat and free of folds, with clean coverslips mounted without bubbles and mounting medium not overflowing the edges. Remove pen marks from the scan area, clean the slide, and use readable barcodes. For fluorescence scanning, use antifade mounting and avoid autofluorescent mounting media; for multiplex panels, plan spectral separation or cyclic staining.
tips: Review the tissue detection and focus point placement on the macro image; faint or fatty tissue is often missed.
Add focus points on difficult tissue or use a denser focus map; rescan out-of-focus slides automatically with QC tools.
Use consistent staining protocols and include a colour calibration slide; apply stain normalisation (Macenko, Reinhard) before analysis.
Store images in open or DICOM formats and keep metadata (pixel size, objective, scanner) with the image.
Validate algorithms on slides from different scanners and sites to test generalisation.
pitfalls: Out-of-focus regions: blurry tiles or strips, often at tissue edges or folds.
Stitching seams or banding from tile misalignment or uneven illumination.
Missed tissue: small fragments outside the detected area.
Air bubbles, dust, pen marks and coverslip edges that confuse analysis and AI.
Confounding in AI: models learning scanner, site or stain differences rather than biology.

history.event: Late 1990s: the first commercial 'virtual microscopy' whole-slide systems appear (e.g. Bacus Laboratories), followed by line-scanning instruments such as the Aperio ScanScope in the early 2000s.
College of American Pathologists publishes guidelines for validating WSI for diagnostic use.
US FDA authorises the first whole-slide imaging system (Philips IntelliSite) for primary diagnosis.
QuPath released as open-source digital pathology software.
Coudray and colleagues predict lung cancer subtype and mutations from H&E with deep learning.
Campanella and colleagues train clinical-grade weakly supervised models on tens of thousands of slides.

quiz.q: Why is focus the main challenge in whole-slide scanning?
quiz.a: At 20-40× with NA 0.75-0.95 the depth of field is ~1 µm, while a section on a slide varies by several micrometres in height over centimetres because of tissue unevenness, folds and slide tilt. Scanners need dense focus maps or real-time focus tracking, and QC to rescan blurred regions.

quiz.q: What does '40×' mean for a scanned slide?
quiz.a: It is a sampling convention, typically ~0.25 µm per pixel, not necessarily a 40× objective. The useful resolution depends on objective NA and focus; a 20× NA 0.75 objective with a 2× tube lens can produce '40×' pixel size.

quiz.q: How would you make a deep learning model robust across hospitals?
quiz.a: Train on diverse sites and scanners, use stain normalisation or colour augmentation, hold out whole sites for testing, check for confounders (e.g. site correlates with label), and calibrate and monitor performance after deployment.

quiz.q: How do you quantify DAB staining from RGB images?
quiz.a: Convert to optical density and use colour deconvolution with stain vectors for haematoxylin and DAB; OD is proportional to stain amount (Beer-Lambert), though DAB is not strictly stoichiometric, so scores are semi-quantitative.

tagline: Imaging cells and tissues inside living animals, usually by multiphoton microscopy through surgical windows, to watch physiology, immunity, cancer and neural activity in their native environment.
principle: Intravital microscopy (IVM) studies biology where it happens: in intact tissue with blood flow, innervation, immune cells and mechanical forces. The main obstacles are light scattering and absorption in tissue, and motion from breathing, heartbeat and peristalsis.

Multiphoton excitation is the workhorse. Two-photon absorption scales with the square of intensity, so excitation is confined to the focal volume and scattered emission photons can all be collected by a large-area (non-descanned) detector. Near-infrared light (~700-1100 nm for two-photon, ~1300 or ~1700 nm for three-photon) scatters less than visible light. Imaging depth in mouse cortex is ~0.5-1 mm for two-photon and ~1-1.5 mm for three-photon.

Ballistic (unscattered) excitation light decays as exp(−z/ℓs), where the scattering length ℓs is ~50-200 µm in brain at relevant wavelengths. Two-photon signal from the focus therefore falls as exp(−2z/ℓs) and must be compensated by increasing laser power until out-of-focus background near the surface or heating limits depth.

Optical access is created surgically: cranial windows or thinned-skull preparations for brain, dorsal skinfold chambers, abdominal or mammary imaging windows for tumours and organs, and exteriorised organs (lymph node, liver, intestine) under anaesthesia. Chronic windows allow imaging the same cells over weeks to months.

Physiological motion must be minimised and corrected: stabilisation by coverslips, suction or gluing, gating acquisition to heartbeat or ventilation, and post-hoc rigid and non-rigid (piecewise) registration. Axial (z) motion cannot be fully corrected after acquisition and must be minimised mechanically or tracked with fast volumetric imaging.

Emitted fluorescence is collected by the same objective and reflected by a dichroic to non-descanned GaAsP photomultipliers close to the objective.

quiz.q: Why is two-photon microscopy preferred for imaging deep in living tissue?
quiz.a: Excitation scales with intensity squared, so fluorescence comes only from the focus and all emitted photons, even scattered ones, are useful signal collected by non-descanned detectors. Near-infrared excitation scatters less, and there is no out-of-focus photobleaching. Depth reaches ~0.5-1 mm in cortex.

quiz.q: What limits two-photon imaging depth and how does three-photon help?
quiz.a: Ballistic excitation decays as exp(−z/ℓs), so power must rise exponentially; eventually out-of-focus fluorescence generated near the surface swamps the signal (signal-to-background limit) or heating limits power. Three-photon excitation at ~1300 or 1700 nm has longer ℓs and cubic intensity dependence, which suppresses surface background, extending depth to ~1.5 mm.

quiz.q: How do you deal with motion in intravital imaging?
quiz.a: Mechanically stabilise (head fixation, window, coverslip pressure, suction), gate acquisition to breathing or heartbeat, acquire fast (resonant scanning), then register frames rigidly or piecewise. Check for z motion, which cannot be corrected in 2D and can mimic activity, using a structural channel or volumetric acquisition.

quiz.q: Resonant or galvo scanning?
quiz.a: Resonant scanners (8-12 kHz lines) give ~30 Hz frames for calcium imaging but fixed line rate and short pixel dwell. Galvo-galvo scanning is slower but allows arbitrary paths, longer dwell, line scans and targeted photostimulation.

tagline: Head-mounted miniature microscopes record neural activity in freely moving animals, while large-field mesoscopes image thousands of neurons across many brain areas at once.
principle: A one-photon miniscope is a ~2-4 g epifluorescence microscope mounted on the head of a mouse or rat. An LED excites a calcium indicator such as GCaMP, a gradient-index (GRIN) lens or small achromat images the tissue, and a CMOS sensor records ~0.5-1 mm fields at 20-30 frames per second. Because there is no optical sectioning, out-of-focus and neuropil background is large and must be removed computationally.

GRIN lenses have a radially varying refractive index that bends light along sinusoidal paths, so a thin rod (0.5-1 mm diameter) can relay an image from deep structures such as hippocampus, striatum or hypothalamus to the surface. Implanting them damages overlying tissue, and they have strong off-axis aberrations and low effective NA (~0.5).

Two-photon miniscopes deliver femtosecond pulses through hollow-core or photonic-crystal fibres and scan with a MEMS mirror, adding optical sectioning and better resolution in freely moving animals at the cost of complexity. Open-source designs (UCLA Miniscope, Finchscope and others) made one-photon miniscopes widely available.

Mesoscopes take the opposite route: large, low-magnification high-NA optics with fields of view of 3-5 mm or more, imaging many cortical areas simultaneously at cellular resolution in head-fixed animals. The key constraint is the optical invariant (étendue): designing an objective with both a large field and high NA requires large, carefully corrected optics. Fast scanning schemes (remote focusing, temporally multiplexed beams, light beads microscopy) increase the number of neurons sampled per second.

Signal extraction is a core part of the method: motion correction, then constrained non-negative matrix factorisation (CNMF, and CNMF-E for one-photon data with large background) or similar algorithms to find spatial footprints and deconvolve calcium traces into estimated spike rates. Registering cells across days enables longitudinal studies of learning and memory.

quiz.q: What are the main limitations of one-photon miniscope data and how are they handled?
quiz.a: No optical sectioning, so large, spatially varying background and neuropil fluorescence overlap the somata; low resolution leads to overlapping cells. Use background-aware source extraction (CNMF-E), careful motion correction, conservative cell selection and validation against two-photon data where possible.

quiz.q: Why would you choose a miniscope over head-fixed two-photon imaging?
quiz.a: When the behaviour requires free movement (social interaction, navigation, sleep, feeding) or the target is deep and reachable only with a GRIN lens. Head-fixed two-photon gives better resolution, sectioning and access to subcellular signals.

quiz.q: What makes mesoscope design hard?
quiz.a: The étendue: maintaining high NA over a millimetre-scale field requires large, well-corrected optics, big scan angles and fast scanning to sample the huge number of resolvable points at a useful frame rate.

quiz.q: How do you track the same neurons across days?
quiz.a: Use a fixed baseplate and consistent focus, register mean or correlation images across sessions, then match footprints by centroid distance and spatial correlation with probabilistic models (e.g. CellReg), reporting match confidence.

tagline: A deformable mirror or spatial light modulator pre-distorts the wavefront to cancel aberrations introduced by the sample, restoring diffraction-limited resolution and brightness deep in tissue.
principle: Microscope objectives are designed for an ideal sample: a specific coverslip thickness and an immersion medium matching the specimen. Real tissue has refractive index variations (cells, nuclei, lipids, vessels) and mismatches with the immersion medium, which distort the wavefront. The focus spreads, peak intensity drops and resolution and contrast degrade, increasingly with depth.

Aberrations are described as a phase function over the objective pupil, conveniently expanded in Zernike polynomials, an orthogonal set over the unit circle. Low orders correspond to familiar aberrations: tip and tilt (shift), defocus, astigmatism, coma, trefoil and primary spherical aberration. Refractive index mismatch mainly produces spherical aberration that grows linearly with depth.

The Strehl ratio, the peak intensity of the aberrated focus relative to the ideal, summarises image quality; the Maréchal approximation links it to RMS wavefront error, and a Strehl ratio above 0.8 (RMS error below ~λ/14) is conventionally 'diffraction limited'. In nonlinear microscopy the signal depends on the square or cube of focal intensity, so aberrations reduce signal even more and correcting them gives large gains.

Adaptive optics (AO) measures the aberration and applies the opposite phase with a corrective element conjugate to the pupil: a deformable mirror (continuous membrane or MEMS, tens to thousands of actuators, fast, achromatic) or a liquid-crystal spatial light modulator (many pixels, slow, polarisation and wavelength dependent, needs phase wrapping). Direct wavefront sensing uses a Shack-Hartmann sensor and a guide star (a fluorescent bead, a two-photon excited spot or a fluorescent protein); indirect or sensorless methods optimise an image metric while applying trial modes, or use pupil segmentation.

Corrections are only valid within an isoplanatic patch, a region over which the aberration is similar, typically tens to a hundred micrometres in tissue. Larger fields need multiple corrections or conjugation of the corrector to the aberrating layer. AO is now used in two-photon and three-photon in vivo imaging, lattice light-sheet microscopy of embryos, super-resolution microscopy deep in cells, and was first developed for astronomy and retinal imaging.
light_path: Laser or light source enters the microscope.
Corrective element (deformable mirror or SLM) placed at a plane conjugate to the objective back pupil via relay lenses.
Scanning optics (if any), also conjugate to the pupil.
Objective focuses light into the sample where tissue aberrates the wavefront.
Wavefront measurement: a Shack-Hartmann sensor views a guide star through a descanned path, or the system evaluates image metrics for sensorless correction.
Control loop computes mode coefficients (Zernike or mirror modes) and updates the corrector, then images are acquired with the correction applied.

equations.name: Zernike expansion of the pupil phase
equations.formula: φ(ρ, θ) = Σ aⱼ Zⱼ(ρ, θ)
equations.meaning: Wavefront over the normalised pupil written as a sum of orthonormal Zernike modes (Noll index j): Z₄ defocus, Z₅-Z₆ astigmatism, Z₇-Z₈ coma, Z₉-Z₁₀ trefoil, Z₁₁ primary spherical.

equations.name: RMS wavefront error
equations.formula: σ = √(Σ aⱼ²) (excluding piston, with orthonormal modes)
equations.meaning: Because Zernike modes are orthonormal, the total RMS error is the root-sum-square of the coefficients.

equations.name: Maréchal approximation for the Strehl ratio
equations.meaning: Strehl ratio S from RMS wavefront error σ; σ = λ/14 gives S ≈ 0.8, the conventional diffraction-limited threshold.

equations.name: Nonlinear signal penalty
equations.meaning: Multiphoton signal depends on peak intensity raised to the order of the process, so a Strehl of 0.5 can cut two-photon signal by about four-fold.

equations.name: Primary spherical aberration from index mismatch
equations.meaning: Spherical aberration grows linearly with focusing depth d into a medium with index n₂ different from the design index n₁, worse at high NA.

Improves super-resolution and light-sheet performance in real samples.
Corrects instrument aberrations and refractive index mismatch automatically.

Calibrate the corrector (influence functions, mode-to-actuator matrix) and remove system aberrations with a bead before measuring sample aberrations.
Use enough photons for the wavefront measurement; noisy measurements apply wrong corrections.
Measure corrections at several positions across the field and depth to map the isoplanatic patch.
Report imaging with and without AO in the same location as a control.
pitfalls: Over-correction or wrong sign: images get worse or features shift because tip, tilt and defocus modes move the focus.

Mistaking brightness improvements for resolution improvements; check PSF or spine size measurements.
SLM artefacts: zero-order spots, polarisation sensitivity and phase-wrapping diffraction losses.
Bias in sensorless metrics optimising for brightness from out-of-focus structures.

quiz.q: What is the Strehl ratio and how does it relate to wavefront error?
quiz.a: The ratio of peak focal intensity with aberrations to that of a perfect system. By the Maréchal approximation S ≈ exp(−(2πσ/λ)²); S ≥ 0.8, or σ ≤ λ/14, is considered diffraction limited.

quiz.q: Which aberration dominates when imaging deep into a watery sample with an oil objective, and how do you fix it?
quiz.a: Primary spherical aberration from refractive index mismatch, growing linearly with depth. Use a water or silicone immersion objective, adjust the correction collar, or correct Zernike spherical modes with AO; also note the axial focal shift distorts z scaling.

quiz.q: Compare direct wavefront sensing and sensorless AO.
quiz.a: Direct sensing with a Shack-Hartmann sensor and a guide star is fast and quantitative but needs a bright point-like source and a descanned path, and is confused by scattering. Sensorless AO applies trial modes and maximises an image metric; it needs no extra hardware but costs exposures and time, and depends on the metric.

quiz.q: Deformable mirror or SLM?
quiz.a: Deformable mirrors are fast, achromatic, polarisation independent and efficient but have fewer actuators and limited stroke. SLMs have many pixels and can shape complex fields but are slow, polarisation and wavelength dependent, and require phase wrapping with diffraction losses.

tagline: A microlens array records both the position and direction of light rays in a single camera frame, so a whole 3D volume can be reconstructed from one snapshot at the cost of lateral resolution.
principle: A conventional camera integrates over all ray angles at each pixel and so loses depth information. A light-field microscope (LFM) places a microlens array at the native image plane and the camera at the microlens focal plane. Each microlens samples a spatial position, and the pixels behind it sample ray angles (the pupil). The 4D light field L(x, y, u, v) is recorded in one exposure.

From the light field, images can be refocused computationally to different depths or viewed from different perspectives. Because the whole volume is captured at once, volume rate equals camera frame rate, which makes LFM attractive for fast volumetric imaging such as whole-brain calcium imaging in larval zebrafish or C. elegans.

The price is a fundamental trade-off: the camera's pixels are shared between spatial and angular sampling. With Nu × Nu pixels behind each lenslet, lateral resolution in the native design is set by the lenslet pitch, coarser than the camera pixel by a factor of Nu, while the number of distinguishable depths is roughly Nu. This is the space-bandwidth product of the sensor being redistributed, not created.

Wave-optics models and 3D deconvolution (Broxton et al.) recover more lateral resolution than lenslet pitch by exploiting aliasing between views, but resolution becomes depth dependent and artefacts appear near the native focal plane where angular diversity is lost. Fourier light-field microscopy places the lenslet array at a pupil plane, giving more uniform resolution and simpler, shift-invariant reconstruction.

Reconstruction is computationally heavy (iterative Richardson-Lucy with a depth-varying PSF), which motivated GPU implementations, sparse decomposition and deep-learning networks that reconstruct volumes in milliseconds. Scanning light-field and digital adaptive optics variants trade some speed for higher resolution and aberration correction.
light_path: Widefield fluorescence excitation of the whole volume (or a selective volume illumination for less background).
Objective and tube lens form an image at the native image plane.
Microlens array at the native image plane (conventional LFM) or at a conjugate pupil plane (Fourier LFM).
Each lenslet forms a small image of the pupil; the f-number of the lenslets is matched to the image-side f-number so these sub-images tile without overlap.
Camera at the lenslet focal plane (often via relay lenses) records the raw light field.
Computational reconstruction (refocusing, 3D deconvolution or neural networks) produces the volume.

equations.name: Space-bandwidth trade-off
equations.meaning: Spatial samples N_s times angular samples N_u is fixed by the sensor; doubling angular sampling halves spatial sampling.

equations.name: Native lateral sampling
equations.meaning: Lenslet pitch divided by magnification sets the native lateral sampling in the sample, e.g. 125 µm / 40 = 3.1 µm.

equations.name: Angular samples
equations.meaning: Number of pixels behind each lenslet; roughly equals the number of resolvable depth planes in the simple geometric picture.

equations.name: f-number matching
equations.meaning: Lenslet f-number must match the image-side f-number of the objective so pupil images fill but do not overlap.

key_numbers.value: equal to camera frame rate (tens to hundreds of volumes/s)

Simple, inexpensive hardware addition (microlens array) to a widefield microscope.
Ideal for fast population activity imaging in small transparent organisms.
No scanning, so no motion distortion within a volume.
limitations: Lateral resolution sacrificed for depth information; rarely single-cell in dense scattering tissue.
Reconstruction artefacts, especially near the native focal plane.
Heavy computation for deconvolution of long recordings.
Widefield illumination gives high background and works poorly in scattering tissue.

Fast 3D dynamics such as cardiac beating, blood flow and particle tracking.
Volumetric imaging where speed matters more than resolution.
Hybrid approaches with sparse labelling or computational demixing in mouse cortex.
sample_prep: Transparent or weakly scattering samples work best: larval zebrafish embedded in low-melting agarose, nematodes immobilised in microfluidics or agarose pads, cleared or thin tissues. tips: Match the lenslet f-number to the objective's image-side NA; mismatch causes overlapping or under-filled sub-images.
Place the region of interest away from the native focal plane, or use Fourier LFM, to avoid the reconstruction artefacts there.
Calibrate lenslet centres carefully (rectification); small misregistration ruins reconstructions.
Use selective volume illumination to reduce background from outside the reconstructed volume.
Validate reconstructions against a scanned ground-truth volume (e.g. confocal or light-sheet) of the same sample.
pitfalls: Grid-like or blocky artefacts near the native focal plane.
Ghost copies and spurious structures from incorrect PSF models or misaligned lenslets.
Overconfident deep-learning reconstructions producing plausible but wrong structures outside the training distribution.
Neuronal signals mixed between nearby cells because of coarse resolution.
Scattering in mammalian tissue breaking the ray model.

quiz.q: What is the fundamental trade-off in light-field microscopy?
quiz.a: The sensor's pixels are shared between spatial and angular samples (Ns × Nu = N pixels per dimension). Angular samples give depth information and refocusing range, but lateral resolution is reduced roughly by the number of pixels behind each lenslet, unless recovered partially by wave-optics deconvolution.

quiz.q: Why is light-field popular for zebrafish whole-brain imaging?
quiz.a: Larval zebrafish are small and transparent, and calcium dynamics across the whole brain must be captured simultaneously. LFM records the entire volume in one frame at camera speed with no scanning, so the moderate resolution is an acceptable trade-off.

quiz.q: Why are there artefacts at the native focal plane?
quiz.a: Near the native focal plane each lenslet sees an almost uniform patch of the object, so different views provide nearly no parallax diversity and the problem is under-determined; deconvolution produces grid-like artefacts. Fourier LFM or defocused designs avoid it.

quiz.q: How would you validate a light-field reconstruction?
quiz.a: Image beads and known structures, compare with scanned confocal or light-sheet volumes of the same sample, check depth-dependent resolution, and for activity data compare extracted traces with ground truth from a subset of neurons.

tagline: Microscopes whose designs, parts lists, firmware and control software are openly published, so that anyone can build, modify, repair and verify them at a fraction of commercial cost.
principle: Open hardware applies the logic of open-source software to instruments: the full design (CAD files, optical layouts, electronics, firmware and control code) is published under open licences with build instructions. A microscope is fundamentally a set of lenses, a light source, a detector and some motion control, and the components (machine-vision cameras, LEDs and lasers, stock optics, 3D-printed or machined mounts, microcontrollers) are now cheap and widely available.

Cost matters because many techniques are bottlenecked by access. A commercial light-sheet or super-resolution system can cost several hundred thousand dollars; open designs such as OpenSPIM, mesoSPIM or open single-molecule platforms can be built for a fraction of that, putting advanced imaging in individual labs, teaching labs and low-resource settings. At the other extreme, the Foldscope (a folded-paper microscope costing under a dollar) and the OpenFlexure microscope (3D-printed, with a flexure stage for sub-micrometre motorised positioning) support field diagnostics, education and citizen science.

Reproducibility is a second reason. When the optical path, components and control software are fully documented, others can replicate the instrument, understand exactly what it measures and identify sources of artefacts. Open control software such as µManager (Micro-Manager), Pycro-Manager, ImSwitch and Python-Microscope standardises hardware control and metadata, and open analysis tools (ImageJ/Fiji, napari, CellProfiler, QuPath) close the loop.

Openness also drives innovation and education. Researchers can add or modify modules (a new illumination path, adaptive optics, a different camera) instead of waiting for a vendor, and students learn optics by building. Modular systems such as UC2 (a cube-based toolbox) teach and prototype setups from widefield to light-sheet; open miniscopes (UCLA Miniscope) made freely-moving calcium imaging widespread in neuroscience.

Open hardware has costs: building, aligning and validating an instrument needs time, skill and documentation; safety (lasers, electrical) and regulatory compliance are the builder's responsibility; and long-term maintenance depends on community support. Good projects publish validation data (PSF measurements, calibration), version their designs and build communities around them.

Detection: machine-vision CMOS or Raspberry Pi cameras, or scientific sCMOS for demanding applications.

equations.meaning: Open instruments face the same limit; using a good objective is often the most important single investment.

equations.name: Nyquist sampling with low-cost cameras
equations.meaning: Camera pixel size divided by magnification must be at most half the resolution; small-pixel CMOS sensors (~1-2 µm) allow low magnification.

equations.name: Cost per capability
equations.meaning: Parts are cheap, but build time, validation and upkeep must be included when comparing with commercial systems.

equations.name: Flexure stage step size
equations.meaning: Leadscrew pitch p_thread divided by motor steps per turn N_steps and gear ratio G, scaled by the flexure lever ratio, gives sub-micrometre motion from cheap stepper motors without sliding friction (OpenFlexure-type stages).

strengths: Low cost and wide access, including teaching labs and low-resource settings.
Full transparency for reproducibility and troubleshooting.
Modifiable: new modalities and experiments without vendor constraints.
Educational value; communities share designs, validation data and fixes.
limitations: Building and aligning requires expertise and time; documentation quality varies.
Less robust automation, stability, service and safety certification than commercial systems.
Performance must be validated by the user; results may vary between builds.
Long-term support relies on community activity and funding.
best_for: Labs needing custom modalities (light-sheet, SMLM, TIRF) on a limited budget.
Teaching optics and microscopy through building.
Field diagnostics, global health and citizen science (e.g. malaria or parasite screening).
Automation and integration with lab robotics or long-term incubator imaging.
sample_prep: Identical to the corresponding commercial modality (e.g. cleared tissue for mesoSPIM, embedded embryos for OpenSPIM, stained blood smears for OpenFlexure diagnostics). Additionally plan calibration samples: fluorescent beads for PSF measurement, stage micrometres and resolution targets (USAF 1951) to validate each build.
tips: Start from a well-documented, actively maintained project and its community forum rather than designing from scratch.
Invest in the components that set performance (objective, camera, filters) and save on mounts and motion.
Validate every build with beads and resolution targets and publish the validation alongside the data.
Use open, standard control software (µManager, Pycro-Manager, ImSwitch) so metadata are recorded in OME format.
Follow laser and electrical safety rules; enclose beams and interlock where needed.
Version-control CAD and code, and record the exact versions used in a study.
pitfalls: Unvalidated performance: assuming the build matches the published design without measuring the PSF.
Mechanical drift and thermal instability of printed parts (PLA creep, warping in incubators).
Poor documentation making the instrument irreproducible even within the same lab.
Hidden costs in time and maintenance overlooked in budget comparisons.
Licensing confusion (CERN-OHL, GPL, CC-BY) when modifying or commercialising designs.

quiz.q: Why do open microscopes matter for science?
quiz.a: They lower cost and widen access to advanced modalities, make instruments fully transparent and reproducible, let researchers modify and extend setups quickly, and train people in optics. Examples: OpenSPIM and mesoSPIM for light-sheet, UCLA Miniscope for freely moving calcium imaging, OpenFlexure and Foldscope for low-cost diagnostics and education, µManager for open control.

quiz.q: What would you check before trusting data from a home-built microscope?
quiz.a: Measure the PSF with sub-resolution beads, verify pixel size with a stage micrometre, check drift and stability over the experiment's duration, characterise illumination flatness and detector linearity and noise, and record all component and software versions.

quiz.q: What are the hidden costs of open hardware?
quiz.a: Builder time, alignment and validation, troubleshooting without vendor support, safety compliance, maintenance and the risk that the project or community fades. These should be weighed against the purchase price and flexibility gains.

quiz.q: How does open software support reproducibility?
quiz.a: Tools such as µManager or Pycro-Manager record acquisition parameters as standard OME metadata and allow scripted, shareable acquisition protocols; open analysis pipelines in Fiji, napari or CellProfiler can be rerun exactly by others.
